Titre: From seaweed to opportunity: Creating jobs and transforming livelihoods in coastal Kenya 🌊🌱
Description:
With traditional livelihoods such as fishing and farming facing growing challenges due to climate change, declining natural resources and limited market opportunities, coastal communities in Kwale County are exploring new ways to diversify their income sources.

Seaweed farming and value addition are enabling women and youth to transform locally harvested seaweed into marketable products such as soap, shampoo and lotion, creating new opportunities for entrepreneurship, job creation and improved livelihoods.

Through the Women and Youth Economic Empowerment in Fisheries through Inclusive Market Access (WYFEEMA) programme, Kilimo Trust is supporting communities to strengthen value addition, economic diversification and access markets. These efforts are enabling women and youth to turn their skills and resources into viable businesses and sustainable livelihoods. The programme is led by the AfCFTA Secretariat, TradeMark Africa and the Mastercard Foundation.

Featuring speakers from Norway, the session explores Norway's experiences and lessons learned in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and antimicrobial use (AMU) surveillance in aquaculture, with a focus on sharing knowledge and best practices that may support sustainable aquaculture development in the ASEAN region.

Featuring aerial drone footage of the site and an interview with the company's CEO, the film provides an insight into the facility, its operations and the thinking behind the business.

Titre: Global Challenges Microalgae Could Help Solve | Future of Biotechnology & Environmental Science
Description:
Can microalgae help solve some of the world's biggest scientific and environmental challenges?

Microalgae are microscopic photosynthetic organisms with enormous potential in biotechnology, medicine, environmental protection, renewable energy and sustainable industrial production.

In this video, we explore **13 major research problems and how microalgae-based technologies could provide innovative solutions.**

🔬 **Topics covered in this video:**

1. Pharmaceutical and medicinal biotechnology – Production of bioactive compounds, antioxidants and therapeutic molecules.
2. Sustainable materials and bioplastics – Microalgal biomass as a renewable resource for biodegradable materials.
3. Genetic engineering and vaccine biotechnology – Recombinant antigen production and potential oral vaccines for aquaculture.
4. Food biotechnology and food safety – Microalgae as alternative protein sources.
5. Environmental biotechnology and metal recovery – Biosorption and recovery of valuable metals.
6. Artificial intelligence and bioprocess engineering – Machine learning for microalgae cultivation optimization.
7. Pharmaceutical delivery systems – Microalgae-derived materials for encapsulation and controlled release.
8. Regenerative medicine and wound healing – Photosynthetic oxygen production and innovative wound dressings.
9. Renewable energy biotechnology – Biological hydrogen production using microalgae.
10. Biopharmaceutical manufacturing – Microalgae as recombinant protein production platforms.
11. Mining and mineral-processing biotechnology – Bioflocculation and wastewater treatment.
12. Biomaterials and tissue engineering – Photosynthetic scaffolds and oxygen-generating hydrogels.
13. Environmental remediation – Heavy metal removal from contaminated water.

🌱 **Why is microalgae research important?**

Microalgae can:
- Capture CO₂ through photosynthesis.
- Produce valuable biomass and bioactive compounds.
- Remove nutrients from wastewater.
- Support sustainable protein and bioproduct production.
- Contribute to renewable energy development.
- Provide new opportunities for environmental biotechnology.

🎯 **Who should watch?**

- Microbiology and biotechnology students.
- Microalgae and algal biotechnology researchers.
- Environmental engineers.
- PhD and Master's students.
- Researchers interested in bioengineering and sustainable biotechnology.

The future of biotechnology may be microscopic, but its impact could be enormous.

Titre: Farmers Can’t Kick the Fertiliser Habit. A Seaweed Biostimulant Helps Them Use Less | Zachary Nice
Description:
Zachary Nice is the founder and CEO of Zentide, a Lombok-based climate tech company that makes Kaylix, a seaweed-based biostimulant. Kaylix combines extracts of tropical red and brown seaweeds with selected microbes. It is not a fertiliser: farmers add it to the backpack sprayer they already use, and it helps plants use fertiliser more efficiently, so they can use less. In Zentide's field trials, farmers cut chemical fertiliser by at least 25%, and up to 50%, without losing yield. Zach is American by birth, grew up in Malaysia, and has spent more than twenty years working in Singapore and Indonesia.

We talk about why Indonesian farmers use synthetic fertiliser at about 2.6 times the recommended dose, why inputs eat 50 to 60% of a horticulture farmer's costs, and why smallholders living harvest to harvest can't afford the switch to organic that cost Zach three years of losses on his own farm. Then how Kaylix was designed to fit what farmers already do with no green premium, why yield sells where cost savings don't, demo plots and WhatsApp channels in Sasak, and why Lombok's seaweed and its coastal growing communities sit at the heart of the business. And the founder's half: logistics, restaurants and COVID, the 100x100 venture-building process that led him to seaweed, the chili farmer who used up to ten times the dose, and what it means to sell to people with no margin for error.

Zentide is looking for collaborators in Indonesia and beyond: distributors, plantation owners and agri-input producers who want to add biostimulants to their formulations or trial them on their plantations, and universities that want to research this category of agri-inputs. If that's you, reach out to Zach and the team through https://zentide.co

Titre: 「いつでも」「安定的に」　陸上養殖による高級魚の本格生産開始へ水槽が完成　秋田・男鹿市 (2026/11/17 18:58)
Description:
秋田県男鹿市の温泉施設跡地に水槽が完成し、陸上養殖による魚の生産が本格化します。飲食店での提供やふるさと納税の返礼品にもなると期待されています。

「男鹿なまはげ魚工房」は２０２４年に閉館した「夕日温泉ＷＡＯ」を男鹿市から譲り受け、ＮＴＴ東日本のＩＣＴ技術を使い陸上養殖の実証を始めています。２０トンと５トンの水槽２基が完成し、１７日に見学会が開かれました。ここで養殖する「タマカイ」は高級魚とされるクエの仲間です。水槽には台湾から輸入した稚魚、１６００尾が入っていて、エサやりの方法が紹介されました。約１年間の実証では県水産振興センターの職員や男鹿水族館ＧＡＯの飼育員に指導してもらいながら１４０尾の稚魚を育て、１２２尾が生存しました。重さは１キロから２キロ以上のものもあり個体によってばらつきがあるものの、陸上養殖に必要なノウハウを習得してきました。

男鹿なまはげ魚工房　澤村誉　社長：「ハタハタが獲れなくなって水産業自体が厳しい状況になっている。陸上養殖はいつでも出せる安定的に出せるというメリットもあるし、そういう意味では冬の美味しいお魚として県内の飲食店に定着するような形で出していきたい」

初出荷は２０２７年の予定で、年間の生産量は約３トンを見込んでいます。将来的には水槽を追加するなどして、年間１００トンベースの生産を目指します。県内の飲食店やホテルと連携し、商品の提供や加工品の開発も進め、２０２７年にはふるさと納税の返礼品としての取り扱いを目指します。

Titre: El Biodiésel Mexicano Hecho con AGUA de DRENAJE que Podría ACABAR con la Gasolina | ¿Verdad o Mito?
Description:
En un invernadero de 400 m² en Xalapa, un agua muy turbia queda casi sin nitrógeno, sin fósforo y sin color en solo siete días. Y lo que crece en ella puede terminar convertido en biodiésel. ¿Magia? No: hay un organismo vivo en medio, y sin él nada de esto se entiende.

Datos duros que verás en este video:
• El invernadero de Xalapa mide 400 m² y se divide en tres módulos: una laguna de fitotratamiento de 13,000 litros, un módulo con lechuga de agua que filtra contaminantes del Río Sordo y un módulo de microalgas.
• La acumulación de lípidos alcanzó 38.5 %: casi 4 de cada 10 partes de la biomasa son grasa aprovechable.
• Según lo citado, el rendimiento de aceite de las microalgas es de 100 a 200 veces el de la soya.
• Una microalga crece en menos de 24 horas, mientras que el maíz o la palma tardan semanas.
• La conversión de microalgas a biodiésel puede tardar menos de tres horas.
• Cerca del 45 % de la energía se gasta solo en cosechar las microalgas.
• La energía global para tratar aguas residuales podría subir hasta 44 % en 2030.
• Participan equipos mexicanos del Inecol, la UAM Iztapalapa, la UANL y la UNAM, con socios de España, Italia y Reino Unido.
• El proyecto obtuvo dos premios en el congreso Biorefinery Research y se financió con la convocatoria Sener-Conacyt Sustentabilidad Energética.

En este video te explicamos cómo funciona la transesterificación, por qué el agua no se convierte en combustible sino que sirve como alimento para las algas, qué hace la UNAM con microalgas nativas del Lago de Texcoco, qué otros equipos mexicanos trabajan en Chiapas y Veracruz, y por qué la cosecha es el gran cuello de botella. También respondemos la pregunta del título: ¿funciona de verdad? Spoiler: hay una respuesta doble, y una parte no te la esperas.

También verás por qué esto no es el biodiésel casero de aceite usado de cocina, qué falta para que sea rentable y qué otros productos podrían salir de la misma biomasa, como bioetanol, biometano, biohidrógeno y compuestos útiles para farmacia, acuicultura, suplementos y cosmética.

Cuéntanos en los comentarios: ¿te parece mejor tratar el agua y sacar combustible a la vez, aunque cueste más? ¿Qué obstáculo crees que se resolverá primero, la cosecha o el costo?

Si te gustó este análisis, suscríbete y activa la campanita para no perderte el siguiente video de Patente Mexicana.

Titre: Israel Farms Millions of Fish in the Desert — Can They Feed 10 Million?
Description:
Israel Farms Millions of Fish in the Desert — Can They Feed 10 Million?

In one of the driest regions on Earth, an extraordinary agricultural transformation is taking place. Thousands of fish are being raised in the middle of the desert, using water that most people would consider unsuitable for farming. But this is only the beginning of a much bigger story.

This documentary explores how Israel transformed the Negev Desert into an unexpected center of aquaculture and advanced food production. From the earliest clay-lined fish ponds to modern underground water systems, engineers and farmers discovered ways to turn harsh desert conditions into an opportunity.

You'll discover how ancient underground aquifers provide water for raising fish such as tilapia and barramundi, how advanced Recirculating Aquaculture Systems (RAS) keep fish alive while recycling most of their water, and how specialized bacteria help remove harmful waste from these systems.

But the innovation doesn't stop with fish. We explore how nutrient-rich wastewater is reused to irrigate date palms and olive trees, how shrimp farms operate far from the ocean, and how seaweed cultivation is bringing marine agriculture onto dry land.

Finally, we travel to the Arava Desert near Eilat, where advanced algae production systems grow valuable natural compounds such as astaxanthin.

What began as an experiment in an unforgiving landscape has developed into a fascinating example of how science, engineering, and agricultural innovation can change the way food is produced.

Titre: White is gold! 🧫 | Blue-White Screening
Description:
Children's Day at a biotech campus near Hyderabad! Intern Faizan has two hours to demo insulin-gene bacteria to investors. He crowns the shiny blue colonies and bins the white ones. Out for a duck! Then ten-year-old Kabir asks one question, and Dr. Sravani explains the real science. 🧫

In this story you'll learn:
✅ The plasmid's lacZ gene makes beta-galactosidase, which cuts colourless X-gal and turns the colony blue
✅ Insertional inactivation: the gene goes into lacZ, lacZ breaks, no enzyme, the colony stays white
✅ White = recombinant (gene inside), blue = empty plasmid
✅ Ampicillin only shows the plasmid got in; the colour shows whether the gene got in
✅ The maths: 21 amino acids × 3 = 63 bp; 20 white out of 200 = just 10%

Titre: Ancient Hawaiian Fishponds: How Fish Trapped Themselves Without Modern Technology
Description:
When storms shut down the ocean, how did ancient Hawaiians still have fresh fish?

They built one of the most remarkable food systems in the Pacific: the loko iʻa, or Hawaiian fishpond. Hundreds of them once ringed the islands. They had stone walls up to 1.3 miles long and wooden gates that let young fish in but kept grown fish inside. They used no pumps, no fish food and no machines.

This is the story of how they worked, how they were built, how they nearly vanished, and how Hawaiians are bringing them back today.

00:00 — The storm and the man on the wall

00:00 — The gate, the algae and the mountain-to-sea system

Titre: Seaweed Farming and Aquatic Animal Welfare in Africa | ESR at EAGx Berlin
Description:
How can seaweed farming support coastal livelihoods while offering a viable alternative to fish farming in Africa?

In this video, Wasseem Emam, Founder and Head of Programmes at Ethical Seafood Research (ESR), introduces our work to improve aquatic animal welfare across Africa, with a particular focus on our seaweed farming research in Zanzibar, Tanzania.

The video was featured during Heather Siekkinen's session at EAGx Berlin, which showcased perspectives from African founders working in animal advocacy and food systems.

Wasseem discusses how ESR is exploring practical, locally appropriate approaches to improving aquatic animal welfare and supporting coastal communities, including:

→ Seaweed farming in Zanzibar:Trialling floating seaweed farming systems that could help producers adapt to warming seas and strengthen climate resilience.

→ Alternative livelihoods: Exploring the economic potential of seaweed farming, particularly for women in coastal communities, as an alternative to activities involving aquatic animals.

→ Local seaweed processing: Investigating opportunities to retain more of the value generated by seaweed production within local communities, including emerging work in Madagascar.

→ Fish welfare in African aquaculture: Working with fish farmers in Egypt and Kenya to improve water quality, handling, harvesting and slaughter practices.

→ Policy and industry collaboration: Supporting the development of national aquaculture codes of practice in Kenya and Egypt.

Wasseem also shares how ESR's work has reached more than 1,500 farms across Egypt and Kenya, with an estimated potential impact on 100-200 million fish.

—

About Ethical Seafood Research

Ethical Seafood Research (ESR) is a non-profit organisation working to improve the lives of aquatic animals in the food system through research, education and practical action. 

We collaborate with farmers, researchers, certifiers and governments to advance animal welfare, improve aquaculture practices and build more ethical, sustainable and resilient aquatic food systems. 

From field research and farmer training to digital innovation and policy engagement, our work focuses on creating practical solutions that benefit both aquatic animals and the communities that depend on them.

Titre: पोटाश का पूरा सच। MOP, SOP, PDM and Seaweed potash? कौन सा आपकी फसल के लिए सही?
Description:
लाल पोटाश क्या सच में अलग खाद है? MOP और SOP में असली फर्क क्या है? शीरे से बने पोटाश में कितना K₂O होता है? और सबसे जरूरी: कौन सा पोटाश आपकी फसल, मिट्टी और जेब के हिसाब से सही है?

इस वीडियो में चारों पोटाश (MOP, SOP, लाल पोटाश और शीरे वाला पोटाश) की सीधी, तथ्य-आधारित जांच है, बिना किसी कंपनी के चश्मे के।

⏱ इस वीडियो में:
0:00 चार पोटाश, एक सवाल
0:50 पौधे के लिए पोटाश क्यों जरूरी है
2:20 MOP: K₂O और क्लोराइड
3:30 लाल पोटाश का भ्रम
4:40 SOP: सल्फर और क्लोराइड
6:00 शीरे वाला पोटाश: दावे और सच
7:30 क्लोराइड संवेदनशील फसलें
8:30 कीमत और प्रति किलो K₂O का हिसाब
10:00 कौन सा पोटाश कब चुनें
11:40 समापन

📌 मुख्य बातें:
• लाल पोटाश भी MOP (पोटैशियम क्लोराइड) ही है, रंग आयरन ऑक्साइड से आता है
• MOP में लगभग 60% K₂O और लगभग 45-47% क्लोराइड
• SOP में न्यूनतम 50% K₂O, 17.5% सल्फर, क्लोराइड अधिकतम 2.5% (FCO)
• शीरे वाले पोटाश में न्यूनतम 14.5% K₂O, यानी बराबर पोषण के लिए लगभग 4 गुना वजन
• बोरी की नहीं, प्रति किलो K₂O की कीमत देखें

💰 अनुमानित भाव (अक्टूबर 2026 तक की सार्वजनिक जानकारी):
MOP: ₹1,534-1,975 प्रति 50 kg बोरी
SOP: लगभग ₹2,250-4,250 (कोई सरकारी MRP नहीं, विक्रेता लिस्टिंग के आधार पर)
शीरे वाला पोटाश: लगभग ₹400-500 (कीमत अनिश्चित)
कीमतें राज्य, कंपनी और सीजन के साथ बदलती हैं, खरीदने से पहले अपने डीलर से पूछ लें।

⚠️ जरूरी सूचना: खुराक मिट्टी जांच और अपने क्षेत्र की सिफारिश से तय करें। वीडियो में दिए उदाहरण केवल समझाने के लिए हैं। यह वीडियो किसी कंपनी का प्रचार नहीं है।

Titre: ఏపీలో అద్భుతం! చెట్టు కాదు, సైన్స్ మిషన్! #AlgaeTree #Guntur #AirPurification #MicroAlgae #SmartCity
Description:
Andhra Pradesh has introduced a unique technology that looks like a tree but is actually a science-based air purification system! Called the Algae Tree, this innovative installation has been set up at the historic Gandhi Park in Guntur as a pilot project to help reduce air pollution. Unlike ordinary trees, the Algae Tree has no leaves, branches or shade. Instead, it uses microalgae and advanced technology to absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen through photosynthesis. Standing 4.5 metres tall and occupying just 1.5 metres of space, this system contains 600 litres of water mixed with microalgae. Powered by solar energy, fans draw polluted air into the system, where microalgae absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen. Sensors monitor temperature, pH levels and airflow, while LED lights provide illumination at night to support the algae's activity. According to Guntur Municipal Corporation (GMC), one Algae Tree can absorb as much carbon dioxide as 20 to 25 large trees. The manufacturing company claims that it can absorb approximately 1.5 tonnes of CO2 annually and purify the surrounding air within a 15-metre radius. The project was launched under the Nava Guntur initiative under the leadership of GMC Commissioner K. Mayur Ashok. The installation cost around Rs. 5 lakh, with CSR funding support from Lalitha Group of Hospitals. Mushroom World Umbrella Limited developed the technology after two years of research. However, this technology is not a replacement for natural trees. Trees provide shade, shelter for birds, biodiversity and environmental protection that an Algae Tree cannot offer. Instead, it can serve as an additional solution in places where planting and maintaining large trees is difficult. If this pilot project succeeds, GMC plans to introduce more Algae Trees in parks, colleges, government offices, bus stations and busy road junctions. Can this innovative technology become a new solution for air pollution in Indian cities? Watch the complete video to understand how Guntur's Algae Tree works and what makes it special.

Titre: Hélène Hegaret et Caroline Fabioux : les microalgues toxiques et l'anoxie
Description:
Le deuxième épisode de notre Podcast est en ligne !! 🏄‍♀️ 
 
Dans cet épisode, nous sommes allées à la rencontre de Caroline Fabioux et Hélène Hegaret, un duo de chercheuses qui étudient les efflorescences de microalgues toxique au laboratoire de Laboratoire des sciences
de l'environnement marin (LEMAR) à Brest. Les toxines de ces organismes constitués d'une seule cellule et invisibles à l'œil nu, peuvent parfois se retrouver les poissons et les coquillages qui ont décidé d’en faire leur casse-croûte. Heureusement, de nombreux services de surveillance sont mis en place pour éviter que l’on se fasse empoisonner.  Au-delà de la consommation humaine, ces microalgues peuvent aussi avoir de gros impacts sur l'environnement en constante évolution avec le changement climatique. Dans cet épisode, nous explorons comment la recherche étudie ces petits organismes ainsi que les solutions qui existent pour le secteur de la pêche.

• How one pump circulates water through seven fish ponds.
• Why adding hay to fish ponds encourages beneficial biodiversity.

• How a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) reuses around 90% of its indoor production water.
• How invasive European carp could become a valuable fish feed.

This is a fascinating example of how regenerative farming principles, biological systems and appropriate technology can work together to produce high-quality food.

Whether you're a farmer, landholder, aquaculture producer or simply interested in the future of sustainable food production, there are lessons here for everyone.

Titre: Inside a factory under the sea! 😳
Description:
Join our LIVE Storytelling Workshop on Sunday, 22 November! https://bit.ly/4zhHR4g

My team travelled to Tamil Nadu to see how seaweed is harvested. And here's what we witnessed.

- They tie their sarees tightly, take a deep breath and dive into the sea. In the name of safety, all they have is an eye mask and a pair of slippers.
- Even after an entire day of hard work, a woman can barely harvest 4–5 kilos of seaweed. And her earnings? Less than ₹1,000.
- A middleman buys the seaweed from them at extremely low prices and sells it at several times the price.
- Spending hours in the water every day leads to skin infections. Sometimes, fish even bite their feet.

Seaweed is used in medicines, cosmetics and food products. Yet, the very women who harvest it from the sea don't even know its actual market value.

And here's the biggest irony:

Women do all the work of harvesting seaweed, but they don't have the right to sell it in the market.

We use seaweed in so many everyday products. But do we ever stop to think about who harvests it for us? And at what cost?

Titre: Marine Biotechnology and the Blue Economy (16 Minutes)
Description:
In this video, we explore Marine Biotechnology and the Blue Economy, an exciting intersection of biotechnology, marine science, and sustainable economic development. Marine biotechnology uses organisms and biological resources from oceans and coastal environments to develop innovative products and processes, while the blue economy focuses on creating economic value from marine resources in ways that support ocean health and long-term sustainability. Understanding this relationship is essential for students, researchers, entrepreneurs, policymakers, and anyone interested in sustainable innovation and the future of ocean-based industries. We will cover the following key aspects:

Defining Marine Biotechnology and the Blue Economy: Understanding how marine organisms, genetic resources, enzymes, and biological processes can be transformed into valuable products and services while supporting sustainable economic activities connected to the ocean.

Why Marine Biotechnology Matters: Exploring how the enormous biodiversity of marine ecosystems provides opportunities for discovering new compounds, materials, enzymes, and biological processes with applications across healthcare, food, energy, and industry.

Key Applications of Marine Biotechnology: Examining important areas such as:

Pharmaceuticals and Healthcare: Exploring marine-derived compounds for drug discovery, medical research, diagnostics, and therapeutic applications.

Industrial Biotechnology: Developing marine-derived enzymes, biomaterials, chemicals, and other products that can provide alternatives to conventional resources.
Environmental Biotechnology: Applying biological approaches to pollution management, bioremediation, ecosystem restoration, and environmental monitoring.

Understanding the Blue Economy: Exploring how ocean-based sectors—including fisheries, aquaculture, marine tourism, shipping, renewable ocean energy, biotechnology, and marine conservation—can generate economic value while maintaining healthy marine ecosystems.

Marine Biotechnology as a Driver of Economic Growth: Examining how marine biotechnology can create new industries, products, employment opportunities, research activities, investment opportunities, and innovative business models within the blue economy.

Sustainability and Ocean Conservation: Understanding the importance of responsible marine resource use, biodiversity conservation, sustainable harvesting, ecosystem protection, and the development of technologies that reduce pressure on marine environments.

Marine Genetic Resources and Bioprospecting: Exploring how researchers identify useful genes and compounds from marine organisms and the importance of responsible access, benefit sharing, intellectual property, and international governance.

Challenges and Ethical Considerations: Examining challenges such as marine ecosystem degradation, resource overexploitation, difficulties in cultivating marine organisms, commercialization of genetic resources, regulatory complexity, and ensuring that economic development does not come at the expense of ocean health.

Role of Emerging Technologies: Exploring how genomics, metagenomics, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence, synthetic biology, and advanced cultivation technologies are accelerating the discovery and development of marine-derived products.

Future of Marine Biotechnology and the Blue Economy: Highlighting emerging opportunities in sustainable aquaculture, algae-based products, marine pharmaceuticals, biomaterials, blue carbon, ocean-based biomanufacturing, and innovative approaches to building a more sustainable ocean economy.

By the end of this video, you will have a comprehensive understanding of marine biotechnology and the blue economy, including how marine biological resources can create economic opportunities while supporting sustainability and ocean conservation. Don’t miss the opportunity to discover how the biotechnology of the ocean could help shape the industries, products, and sustainable solutions of the future!

With more than 17,000 islands and a #blueeconomy worth around US$39 billion, Indonesia has significant potential to create greater economic opportunities while protecting its #marine and coastal resources.

In Sidoarjo, East Java, #seaweed farming has become an important source of livelihood for coastal communities. With better cultivation practices, post-harvest facilities and market access, seaweed offers opportunities to improve farmers’ incomes and capture more value locally.

While Indonesia accounts for approximately 69% of global seaweed exports, more than 66% of its exports are still raw or semi-processed. The opportunity is to move beyond production volume towards greater value creation through processing, innovation and product #development.

Through the Archipelagic and Island States (AIS) Forum, the Government of Indonesia and UNDP are working together, with the generous support of the Government of Indonesia and in collaboration with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries, to unlock the blue economy’s potential and strengthen coastal #livelihoods.

Titre: 温暖化に左右されない「ノリの陸上養殖」に九州大学が成功　収穫期間を約10日に短縮　コストも海養殖の1割増程度に抑え商品化へ｜TBS NEWS DIG
Chaîne: TBS NEWS DIG Powered by JNN
Description:
シリーズSDGs「地球を笑顔にするWEEK」です。日本の伝統食・ノリの養殖は浅い海で行われるだけに、海水温の上昇の影響を受けます。温暖化の影響を受けないノリの陸上養殖の研究が進んでいます。

佐賀県沖の有明海では先月末、養殖ノリの種付けが行われ、今、ノリ漁師はノリ網の手入れに追われています。今シーズンの出来は期待できそうだということです。

ノリ漁師　藤川直樹さん
「ここ最近例年になく、今のところはいい海況」

ノリ養殖は海水温に影響されます。日本近海の海面水温は2025年までの100年間で1.36℃上昇。世界全体の平均の2倍を超えるペースです。

ノリの種付けは海水温23℃以下が目安ですが、近年は水温がなかなか下がらず、かつては10月1日に始まっていた種付けが去年初めて11月にずれ込みました。

養殖できる期間が短くなったうえ、以前より増えている豪雨による土砂災害も海の環境に打撃を与えています。

ノリ漁師　藤川直樹さん
「豪雨があって一気に雨が流れて、そこで赤潮が出たり、土砂が流れてきて（海の中が）浅くなったり」

記者
「糸島の海から2キロ以上離れたこちらの施設で、ノリの陸上養殖が研究されています」

九州大学は今、温暖化に左右されない屋内型のノリ養殖の研究を進めています。

九州大学　シャハ ビデユット バラン教授
「陸上ですると温度の管理とか他の管理ができれば、年間ずっと育てることができます」

ラボでは、室温も水温もノリの養殖に適した18℃前後に保ち、塩分濃度や光の加減などを研究。特に難しかったのはノリの成長に欠かせない栄養塩づくりでした。

九州大学　シャハ ビデユット バラン教授
「（研究は）2年以上です。いろいろ組み合わせしながら、5～10種類のいろんなもの。自然由来が多いです。それを入れて栄養塩を作りました」

ノリが収穫できるサイズに育つまで海で養殖する場合は1か月ほどかかりますが、ラボではこれを10日ほどに短縮。使用する海水の確保にも一工夫しています。

九州大学　シャハ ビデユット バラン教授
「黒い布があると光が入らない。（海水が）長持ちになります」

取水した海水を殺菌し光を遮って保管することで、海水の入れ替えを2か月に1回で済むようにしました。

そして、今年9月、九州大学はノリの陸上養殖に成功し、焼き海苔を製造したと発表しました。民間企業と組んで商品化を目指しています。

九州大学　シャハ ビデユット バラン教授
「（これからは養殖の）完全な自動化と栄養の最適化できたものを陸上で作りましたから、もしうまくいけば完全なビジネスも考えています。（Q.日本の食卓にノリが届く可能性も?）そう思っています。それなら一番うれしく思っています」

陸上養殖のノリの生産コストは一般的な海での養殖より10%ほど高い程度。温暖化から日本の食文化を守る陸上養殖のノリが店頭に並ぶ日も、そう遠くないかも知れません。

Titre: Microalgues au microscope (Chlamydocapsa, Chlamydomonas ?) - 100x immersion d'huile + encre de Chine
Description:
Microalgue d'eau douce en cours d'identification, possiblement Chlamydocapsa ou un stade précoce de Chlamydomonas. Cellules souvent par groupe de 4 qui se divisent elles-mêmes en 4 (parfois 8) et ainsi de suite. Mise en évidence d'un mucilage gélatineux autour des cellules grâce à l'encre de Chine (mouvement brownien très visible !). Pas de tractus (filaments) entre les cellules. La taille des cellules varie fortement selon le stade, de 5µm à 17µm (voir 20µm). Vacuole contractile d'un seul côté, et pyrénoide bien visible.

Vidéo filmée avec un smartphone Samsung Galaxy A35 5G (zoom 1x, 2x et 4x) à l'oculaire d'un microscope Olympus CX21 avec un objectif UIS Plan 100x/1.25 à immersion d'huile. Encre de Chine + illumination oblique.

Titre: Catalyzing Marine Finfish Aquaculture Through Public Aquariums | AIE Webinar
Description:
Session Description
Public aquariums have unique opportunities to advance marine finfish aquaculture through their animal collections, technical expertise and capacity for research and innovation. Through the NOAA Sea Grant-funded project “Catalyzing Marine Finfish Aquaculture Through Public Aquariums,” a national network of public aquariums and academic institutions has worked to overcome persistent challenges in marine fish breeding and larval rearing.

This webinar will highlight the development of this collaborative network, technical advances achieved through shared expertise and the successful breeding and rearing of more than 20 marine fish species. We will discuss successes and challenges in broodstock management, egg collection, larval nutrition and juvenile production, as well as opportunities for technology transfer, workforce development and expanding marine aquaculture beyond public aquarium collections.

Breeding and Raising Fish for Aquariums StoryMap: https://arcg.is/1vuq0z3 

Speaker Bio
Dr. Andrew L. Rhyne is a professor of marine biology at Roger Williams University in Bristol, Rhode Island. His research focuses on marine aquaculture, larval culture, aquarium fisheries and the sustainability of the global aquarium trade. His work integrates applied aquaculture research with commercial production, public aquarium partnerships and conservation science. Through a longstanding partnership between Roger Williams University and the New England Aquarium, he has helped expand aquaculture research and production within public aquariums, including the recent completion of a NOAA Sea Grant-funded project focused on advancing marine finfish aquaculture through collaborative research and technology development.

Titre: Norway's AI Robots Use Lasers to Save Salmon! 🤖🐟
Description:
Norway is using thousands of AI-powered underwater robots equipped with precision lasers to protect farmed salmon from sea lice. Developed by Norwegian company Stingray Marine Solutions, the technology uses underwater cameras and artificial intelligence to detect parasites attached to fish. Once identified, a green laser targets and eliminates the lice without harming the salmon.

Sea lice are a major problem in fish farming because they can damage fish skin, cause infections, and even lead to death. Traditional treatments can also stress or injure the fish. Stingray's robots work 24/7 inside fish cages, detecting and removing parasites without taking the salmon out of the water. The system has reportedly helped protect more than 100 million salmon and trout, showing how AI and laser technology can make fish farming safer and more efficient.

Titre: Kelp Farming in Alaska: Outplanting and Harvesting
Description:
Kelp farming in Alaska requires careful planning, seasonal monitoring, and hands-on work in the marine environment. In this video, Chugach Regional Resources Commission (CRRC) and the Alutiiq Pride Marine Institute (APMI) demonstrate the process of outplanting hatchery-grown kelp seed string onto growlines, monitoring kelp throughout the winter growing season, and harvesting mature kelp in the spring. These activities are part of CRRC's multi-year kelp mariculture research project, which has evaluated cultivation techniques, environmental conditions, and kelp growth at research and commercial sites throughout Prince William Sound and Lower Cook Inlet.

Funded by the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Trustee Council (EVOSTC), this project supports the development of practical kelp farming knowledge and sustainable economic opportunities for Tribal and coastal communities in the spill-affected region.

Titre: From Training to Employment | Strengthening the Global Maritime Workforce
Description:
The future of maritime competitiveness will increasingly depend on a skilled workforce, specialised expertise, and institutional capabilities that enable countries to create value beyond physical infrastructure. From maritime analytics and risk management to regulatory expertise, marine advisory services, environmental assessment, certification, and technical services, knowledge-intensive professions are becoming critical to the global maritime economy. 

While established maritime hubs have built strong talent ecosystems in these areas, many emerging economies remain dependent on external expertise. Investing in maritime education, vocational training, professional development, and specialised institutions can help countries build domestic capabilities, generate high-value employment, and participate more effectively in global maritime value chains. 

This session examines how governments, industry, and academia can strengthen maritime skilling ecosystems to build a future-ready workforce for the ocean economy.

Titre: Cultivating The Future: Kelp Farming with Jorunn Skjermo
Description:
Send us Fan Mail (https://www.buzzsprout.com/2258149/fan_mail/new) 


Kelp is having a moment, but not for the reason most people think. It grows astonishingly fast, builds huge biomass, and pulls carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere as it grows. So far so good - the hard part is making sure that carbon does not simply bounce straight back into the carbon cycle. 


In this episode we talk to Jorunn Skjermo, Senior Research Scientist at SINTEF, to unpack what seaweed-based carbon removal could look like in the real world and what has to be true for it to deliver genuine climate positive outcomes. 

We start with the basics of kelp farming and then focus in on SINTEF’s Seaweed Carbon Solutions work around offshore Norway. Jorun explains why offshore sites can be more productive, how nutrient-rich currents drive growth, and what the team learns when they move beyond sheltered waters into harsher conditions. 


We also talk about the ocean itself: how kelp farms can create habitat for crustaceans and fish, how large-scale seaweed farming may reduce local acidification, and where optimism about ecosystem restoration meets the limits of ocean warming and pollution. 

Then we get practical about permanent carbon storage, look squarely at the awkward truths on claiming negative emissions, and explore solutions like reusing steel, electric vessels, and using excess heat from other industries, plus a provocative idea about repurposing retired oil rigs. 

If you love climate tech, ocean science or the wonderful world of seaweed, this is an episode for you!

Titre: XI-Biotechnology Chapter 1: Introduction to Biotechnology
Description: Biotechnology merges biological systems with technology to generate useful products for humanity, spanning from ancient practices like fermentation and selective breeding to modern advancements. The field has evolved through significant historical milestones, including the invention of microscopes, the establishment of cell theory, and the discovery of DNA as genetic material. Modern biotechnology relies heavily on recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology, which allows scientists to manipulate genes and transfer them between organisms with high precision. This multidisciplinary approach impacts various sectors, categorized into areas like blue biotechnology for marine applications, green biotechnology for agriculture, red biotechnology for medicine, and white biotechnology for industrial processes. Ultimately, these techniques drive critical innovations in medicine, healthcare, agriculture, food processing, and environmental protection.

Titre: 일본 말고 아무도 못 한 장어 양식을 한국이 세계 두 번째로 해낸 소름 돋는 이유
Description:
※ 본 영상은 공개 자료를 바탕으로
엔터테인먼트 목적으로 재구성했습니다.

일본 말고 아무도 못 한 장어 양식을 한국이 세계 두 번째로 해낸 소름 돋는 이유를 알아봅니다.

우리가 먹는 민물장어는 대부분 바다에서 강으로 올라오는 투명한 새끼, 실뱀장어를 잡아 한두 해 키운 것입니다. 장어는 알을 낳을 때가 되면 필리핀 동쪽 마리아나 해구 근처의 먼 바다까지 헤엄쳐 가는 독특한 생태 때문에, 사람 손으로 알을 받아 키우기가 매우 어려운 물고기입니다. 그래서 2012년 무렵 실뱀장어 1킬로그램은 3천5백만 원으로 금값에 맞먹었고, 국내에서 필요한 30톤 가운데 자연에서 잡히는 양은 1.5톤뿐이었습니다. 이 일을 해낸 나라는 40년을 연구한 일본뿐이었죠. 국립수산과학원은 대나무 잎처럼 납작하고 투명한 장어 유생을 약 250일 동안 키워야 하는 벽에 도전했고, 2012년 수조에서 부화한 새끼를 실뱀장어로 키워내는 데 성공했습니다. 2016년 해양수산부는 이 실뱀장어를 4년 동안 어미로 키워 2세대 새끼 10만여 마리를 얻었다며, 일본에 이어 세계 두 번째로 완전양식 기술을 개발했다고 발표했습니다. 대량 생산은 아직 숙제로 남아 양식 종자의 70% 이상을 여전히 수입에 기대고 있지만, 2025년 전남 해양수산과학원이 인공 종자 66마리를 생산하며 국내 두 번째 성공을 기록했고, 지금은 대학 연구소까지 힘을 합쳐 양식장 대량 생산의 길을 찾고 있습니다.

Description:
세계에서 김을 기르는 바다가 가장 넓은 나라는 중국입니다. 그런데 지난해 한국 마른김을 가장 많이 사 간 나라도 바로 중국이었습니다.
같은 김이 아니기 때문입니다. 중국 남쪽 바다의 김은 두꺼워서 국에 넣어 먹고, 한국 김은 얇게 한 장으로 떠서 김밥을 말거나 기름과 소금을 발라 구워 먹습니다.

100년 전 한국 김은 일본 밥상에 올리려고 실려 가던 원료였습니다.
김의 씨가 조개껍데기 속에서 온다는 걸 밝힌 영국의 과학자, 그 발견을 붙잡아 먼저 달려 나간 일본, 그리고 그물을 넓은 바다에 띄워 따라잡은 한국.
그 김을 불 위에서 다시 만든 조미김은 이제 미국 마트의 간식이 됐고, 수입 한도를 정해 둔 일본도, 김 바다가 가장 넓은 중국도 사 갑니다.
2025년 한국 김 수출은 11억 3천만 달러, 수산식품 하나로는 처음으로 10억 달러를 넘었습니다.
원료를 대던 바다가 어떻게 세계가 사 가는 김을 만들게 됐는지, 그리고 따뜻해지는 바다 앞에서 다음 한 장은 어디서 나올지 지식부엉이와 함께 따라가 봅니다. 🦉

Titre: SANDY V2: Um Fotobiorreator Inteligente com Controle de Luz! 🌱🔬 | Microalgae Research
Description:
SANDY V2 — Fotobiorreator de baixo custo com controle programável de iluminação

O SANDY (Smart Algal Nutrient & Light DeliverY system) é um fotobiorreator de bancada desenvolvido em nosso grupo de pesquisa para o cultivo de microalgas, com foco em Dunaliella salina. O projeto surgiu com o objetivo de desenvolver uma alternativa acessível, modular e customizável para pesquisas em cultivo de microalgas, utilizando impressão 3D, materiais de fácil acesso e componentes comerciais.

Dando continuidade ao desenvolvimento da primeira versão, o SANDY V2 incorpora um sistema eletrônico de controle da intensidade luminosa por PWM (*Pulse Width Modulation*), permitindo ajustar a potência dos LEDs e desenvolver diferentes perfis de iluminação de acordo com as necessidades experimentais.

Entre os avanços desta versão, destacam-se:

🔸Controle de intensidade luminosa: ajuste eletrônico da potência dos LEDs, com testes de funcionamento em diferentes níveis de acionamento (duty cycle).

🔸Programação do fotoperíodo: desenvolvimento de um sistema capaz de executar ciclos de iluminação programáveis, incluindo a demonstração de um ciclo de 24 horas em 24 segundos.

🔸Caracterização da distribuição luminosa: realização de medições preliminares em diferentes posições e alturas ao redor do compartimento de cultivo, permitindo investigar a distribuição espacial da luz no sistema.

A versão 2 ainda está em desenvolvimento, e os resultados apresentados representam etapas preliminares de implementação e caracterização. As próximas melhorias envolvem o aprimoramento da distribuição luminosa e a investigação de novas possibilidades de automação e monitoramento das condições de cultivo.

Além de apresentar a evolução do equipamento, o projeto busca incentivar o compartilhamento de soluções científicas acessíveis, permitindo que outros pesquisadores conheçam a proposta, reproduzam o sistema e contribuam para seu aperfeiçoamento.

Os arquivos de modelagem 3D e a documentação da primeira versão do projeto estão disponíveis publicamente no Zenodo. O desenvolvimento da V2 dá continuidade a essa proposta de compartilhamento e aprimoramento colaborativo.

🔗 Acesse os arquivos do projeto no Zenodo:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23375435

https://molino-algae.github.io/justlab-site/

Agradecimentos

Agradeço também ao laboratório parceiro BIOSEP NANOLAB, especialmente ao Prof. Dr. André Moreni Lopes e à Monique Ariane da Silva Santos, pela parceria, colaboração e apoio no desenvolvimento e aprimoramento do SANDY.

Titre: Kelp Grows Half a Metre a Day. Why Don't We Eat It?
Description:
Giant kelp can grow up to half a metre in a single day, with no soil, no fresh water and no fertilizer. People were already using seaweed as food around 14,000 years ago at Monte Verde in Chile, and yet for most of us it never reaches the plate. Most people assume it tastes awful or is unsafe. That is not quite right, and the real answer has nothing to do with taste.

You will see how the British botanist Kathleen Drew-Baker solved the mystery of nori in 1949, why Japan makes roughly 6 to 7 billion nori sheets a year, how Scottish and Irish kelp was burned for soda in the 1700s and led to the discovery of iodine in 1811, and why the Great Famine of 1845 to 1849 gave seaweed a stigma. Global farming is about 36 million tonnes a year, and where a figure is an estimate or differs by source, the video says so.

Titre: Ep 138: Seaweed Farms Between Wind Turbines, and the NIMBY Trap
Description:
Clarice brings Marisa a hot take from Denmark. 

Researchers at Aarhus University are testing whether the open water between offshore wind turbines, which is now treated as a mostly unusable zone, could be used to grow seaweed. 

The article describes it as a reuse story. The seaweed could help absorb nutrient pollution (nitrogen and phosphorus, the drivers of harmful algal blooms), and it could be sold as a food crop, such as sugar kelp.

Marisa hears a warning in that framing. Rhode Island and Virginia fishermen were told they could keep fishing between turbines, with about one nautical mile of spacing. So if Denmark treats those areas as unfit for regular vessel traffic, what does that say about the promises made here?

From there the conversation widens:

- Is the space between turbines becoming the ocean's version of Route 66, a corridor we're scrambling to find a use for?
- Does every leftover space have to become production space, or could rewilding be an option?
- Why do we accept cell antennas on rooftops but resist solar panels there, and push energy infrastructure into deserts and open ocean instead?
- Marisa's central point: "NIMBY" is only ever used as an insult, and it's now used to shut down legitimate conservation objections. If every objection is written off as NIMBYism, the ocean gets industrialized, and people will eventually ask where the conservationists were.

NC Division of Marine  Fisheries: Allegations and Unanswered Questions
Description:
A former North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries employee has raised serious allegations involving fisheries research, allegedly falsified gill-net survey records, flounder management, protected species, and the accuracy of fisheries data.

On September 10, 2026, Chloe Dorin sent a nine-page email to state officials, including Governor Josh Stein, titled “Why I Am Leaving the Division of Marine Fisheries.” She also cited the Coastal Conservation Association's lawsuit against the state and called for consideration of dissolving and rebuilding the Division.

In this Saltwater Report Special Presentation, we examine Dorin's allegations and the original documents.

But there's a second story.

It took nearly a month, repeated inquiries, and a formal public records request to obtain an official copy of Dorin's email. After receiving it, the Saltwater Report submitted five specific questions to the Division concerning fisheries research, data accuracy, management decisions, and federal oversight.

The state issued a general statement describing the claims as “unsubstantiated, misinformed or lacking proper context,” but did not specifically address the individual allegations or answer the five questions. Two follow-up requests also went unanswered as of airtime.

This special presents the allegations, the state's response, the correspondence, and the timeline. Dorin's allegations have not been established as facts. Viewers can examine the evidence and draw their own conclusions.

Titre: Biofilms in Marine Biotechnology | CSIR NET Life Sciences
Description:
🌊🦠 What are marine biofilms? How do microorganisms form biofilms on ship hulls, rocks, marine organisms, and other submerged surfaces? What is their significance in marine biotechnology?

In this lecture, Rupendra Singh Sir explains marine biofilms, their formation, chemical composition, major types, ecological importance, and applications in marine biotechnology. This topic is useful for students preparing for CSIR NET/JRF Life Sciences, CSIR DBT JRF NET, GATE Biotechnology, and UGC NET Environmental Science.

📚 Topics Covered in This Lecture:

What are biofilms?

Definition and characteristics of marine biofilms

How marine biofilms form: major stages of biofilm development

Initial surface conditioning and microbial attachment

Role of bacteria, diatoms, algae, and other microorganisms

Chemical composition of biofilms

Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS): polysaccharides, proteins, extracellular DNA and other components

Structure and organization of marine biofilms

Biofouling and biofilms on ship hulls

Ecological importance of marine biofilms

Beneficial and harmful effects of biofilms

Applications in marine biotechnology

Biofilm-associated corrosion and antifouling strategies

Important concepts for CSIR NET and GATE examinations

🔬 Importance of Marine Biofilms

Marine biofilms play important roles in nutrient cycling, microbial interactions, surface colonization, and marine ecosystem functioning. They can also contribute to biofouling and microbiologically influenced corrosion, while offering opportunities in biotechnology, bioremediation, and the development of novel antifouling technologies.

Titre: Aquaculture Systems
Description:
Aquaculture Systems – An Introduction

Welcome to this lesson on Aquaculture Systems!

Aquaculture is the farming of aquatic organisms such as fish, prawns, crabs, molluscs, and aquatic plants under controlled conditions. It plays a vital role in providing nutritious food, generating employment, and supporting the livelihoods of fishing communities.

Aquaculture systems are broadly classified into three types.

1. Extensive Aquaculture: This system relies mainly on natural food available in the water body, with minimal human intervention. It requires low investment and is commonly practised in ponds and reservoirs.

2. Semi-intensive Aquaculture: This system combines natural food production with supplementary feeding, fertilisation, and regular water-quality management. It offers higher productivity than extensive farming.

3. Intensive Aquaculture: This system involves high stocking densities, formulated feeds, aeration, and close monitoring of water quality. Biofloc technology and Recirculating Aquaculture Systems, or RAS, are examples of advanced approaches used in intensive aquaculture.

Aquaculture can also be practised in freshwater, brackish water, and marine environments, depending on the species being cultured.

In conclusion, sustainable aquaculture systems help meet the growing demand for aquatic food while promoting efficient resource utilisation and environmental protection.

Thank you for watching! Stay curious and continue exploring the fascinating world of Aquaculture.

Description:
🌊📊 AquaBusiness | O futuro da tilápia brasileira e as novas tendências do mercado

O mercado de pescado está mudando. Mas como a cadeia produtiva pode acompanhar as transformações no comportamento do consumidor e ampliar o consumo de pescado no Brasil?

No novo episódio do AquaBusiness, recebemos Elane Correia, Zootecnista, Consultora Técnica Comercial da EC Consultoria e Especialista em Pescado, para uma análise sobre a Seafood Show Latin America 2026, as tendências de mercado e os desafios e oportunidades para o futuro da tilápia brasileira.

🎯 Entre os principais pontos dessa discussão, três oportunidades merecem atenção:

🐟 1. Inovação e praticidade  
Novos produtos, porções adequadas, embalagens funcionais e informações claras sobre conservação e preparo podem tornar o pescado mais acessível e facilitar sua inclusão na alimentação cotidiana.

Diante da concorrência dos produtos importados, é fundamental fortalecer o setor produtivo, destacar a qualidade do pescado nacional, valorizar a eficiência produtiva e ampliar a comunicação sobre a origem do produto.

📈 3. Agregação de valor e conexão com o consumidor  
Mais do que competir pelo preço, a cadeia do pescado precisa compreender as necessidades do consumidor e conectar produção, indústria e varejo para desenvolver soluções que estimulem o consumo.

💡 E qual será o futuro da tilápia brasileira?

A competitividade do setor dependerá cada vez mais da capacidade de inovar, entender o mercado e comunicar o valor do pescado produzido no Brasil.

O desafio não é apenas produzir mais, mas também agregar valor, conquistar o consumidor e ampliar o espaço do pescado na mesa dos brasileiros.

Can shrimp and seaweed farming create new economic opportunities for Bangladesh?

Bangladesh has a large coastal region and access to the Bay of Bengal. Could responsible marine farming help create jobs, support local businesses, strengthen seafood production, and build a more sustainable blue economy?

In this educational documentary, we explore the potential of **integrated shrimp and seaweed farming**. We examine how the system works, what research in Bangladesh and other countries tells us, and what would be needed to develop the industry responsibly.

- What the blue economy means and why the Bay of Bengal is important
- How shrimp farming and seaweed cultivation may work together
- How seaweed can absorb dissolved nutrients under suitable conditions
- What research in Bangladesh and India suggests about integrated aquaculture
- How marine farming could support processing, transport, equipment, and other local businesses
- Why pilot projects, scientific research, and market development must come before large-scale expansion
- What seaweed farming may contribute to environmental management and carbon storage
- Why marine biodiversity, fishing communities, shipping routes, and water quality must be protected

### An important note
This video explores a potential development pathway, not a guaranteed economic forecast. The marine area discussed is a hypothetical scenario, not an estimate of land or ocean that is confirmed suitable for farming. Actual production, revenue, employment, and environmental benefits would depend on scientific testing, investment, market demand, and responsible planning.

Titre: Inside the Feed Mill: Building the Future of Sustainable Aquaculture
Description:
This episode is sponsored by Undercurrent (https://www.undercurrentnews.com/) 


Episode Summary 


Aquaculture feed is far more than a mixture of ingredients. A modern feed mill brings together nutrition science, biology, technology, ingredient sourcing and manufacturing expertise to produce feed tailored to the needs of different species and life stages. Jose Luis Tejedor, CEO of the family-owned Tejedor Lázaro Group and DIBAQ Aquaculture, explains how that process works, from nutritionists developing species-specific formulations to the grinding, mixing, extrusion, drying, cooling and coating processes that transform raw materials into precisely sized pellets. The discussion also highlights why feed is such a significant consideration for farmers, affecting production costs, fish growth, health and feeding performance. 


The conversation also explores how aquaculture feed is evolving as the industry looks for more sustainable and efficient ways to produce nutrition for farmed fish. Feed manufacturers are increasingly exploring alternatives to traditional marine ingredients, including insect meal, bacterial proteins, plant-based proteins and algae, while also placing greater emphasis on responsible ingredient sourcing and deforestation-free supply chains. Advances in feed mill technology, sustainability certifications and nutrition research are helping manufacturers improve efficiency while addressing environmental challenges. Looking ahead, Tejedor sees opportunities in developing feeds for new species, supporting fish health in a changing climate and strengthening the role of feed manufacturers as technical partners to farmers. 


Featured Guests 

  •  Jose Luis Tejedor 
     CEO, Tejedor Lázaro Group and DIBAQ Aquaculture 

Key Topics Covered 

  •  The role of feed mills in modern aquaculture 
  •  How species-specific fish feed formulations are developed 
  •  The process of turning raw ingredients into finished aquaculture feed 
  •  Ingredient sourcing, quality control and traceability 
  •  The evolution of fish meal and fish oil use in aquaculture diets 
  •  Alternative feed ingredients, including insect meal, bacterial proteins, plant proteins and algae 
  •  Advances in extrusion and feed mill technology 
  •  Energy efficiency and more sustainable feed manufacturing 
  •  Sustainability certifications and responsible ingredient sourcing 
  •  Deforestation-free soy and environmental requirements for feed ingredients 
  •  The relationship between feed, fish health, farm performance and production costs 
  •  Future opportunities for aquaculture nutrition and new farmed species 

Key Takeaways 

  •  Fish feed is highly specialized. Feed formulations must account for differences between species, fish size, freshwater and marine environments, and specific nutritional requirements. 
  •  Ingredient quality is fundamental. Even advanced equipment and sophisticated formulations cannot compensate for poor-quality raw materials. 
  •  Aquaculture nutrition is moving beyond traditional marine ingredients. The industry is researching alternatives such as insect meal, bacterial proteins, plant proteins and algae to reduce reliance on fish meal and fish oil. 
  •  Feed mill technology continues to evolve. Manufacturers can improve production by optimizing existing equipment while also investing in machinery that reduces energy consumption and increases productivity. 
  •  Sustainability extends beyond the final feed formula. Responsible sourcing, traceability and considerations such as deforestation-free agricultural ingredients are increasingly important to feed manufacturers and their customers. 
  •  Feed influences more than growth. Nutrition can affect fish health, performance, feeding behavior and ultimately the economics of aquaculture production. 
  •  Feed manufacturers are becoming technical partners. DIBAQ's approach extends beyond selling feed to providing farmers with nutrition, health and production support. 
  •  The next generation of aquaculture nutrition will require continued innovation. New species, alternative ingredients, fish health challenges and environmental pressures will all shape future feed development.

Titre: Bactérias marinhas vencendo as tintas dos navios?
Description:
🚢 BACTÉRIAS RESISTENTES AO COBRE: POR QUE OS NAVIOS SOFREM CADA VEZ MAIS COM BIOINCRUSTAÇÃO?

O cobre é utilizado em tintas anti-incrustantes para proteger os cascos de navios contra a colonização por organismos marinhos. Mas o que acontece quando bactérias conseguem tolerar concentrações elevadas desse metal?

🔬 Um estudo científico publicado em outubro de 2026 na revista Biointerphases investigou como bactérias marinhas sobrevivem em superfícies expostas ao cobre e quais mecanismos genéticos podem explicar essa tolerância.

Os resultados ajudam a compreender um dos desafios da indústria naval: a formação de biofilmes microbianos e sua contribuição para a perda de eficácia de revestimentos anti-incrustantes.



⚓ A DESCOBERTA CIENTÍFICA

Os pesquisadores coletaram biofilmes na Baía de Chesapeake, nos Estados Unidos, utilizando painéis revestidos com tinta à base de cobre e painéis de PVC sem revestimento como controle.

Os ensaios laboratoriais demonstraram elevada tolerância ao cobre entre os isolados bacterianos estudados. A análise genômica também identificou genes associados à resistência e à regulação do cobre.

O estudo destaca que a colonização microbiana pode contribuir para a formação de biofilmes e favorecer a incrustação posterior por outros organismos marinhos.

📌 Os resultados se referem aos microrganismos e às condições experimentais investigadas. O estudo não demonstra que todos os navios estejam sofrendo agravamento da bioincrustação, nem que todas as bactérias sejam resistentes ao cobre.

📚 ARTIGO CIENTÍFICO ORIGINAL

Título: Extreme copper tolerance and genomic adaptation in early-stage marine biofilms

Autores: Kailey N. Richard e colaboradores.

Revista: Biointerphases, volume 21, artigo 051003 (2026).

Data de publicação: 13 de outubro de 2026.

Titre: Marine Biotechnology CSIR NET | Lecture 2 | Advances in Biotechnology
Description:
Marine Biotechnology CSIR NET Lecture 2 covers seafood microbiology, marine pharmacology, biofouling, biofilms and oceanography in depth for CSIR NET Life Science aspirants. 
This is Unit 13 – Advances in Biotechnology, and the video is designed for CSIR NET Life Science Dec 2026 preparation, with practice questions solved at the end.

In this lecture you will learn why stale fish develops a fishy smell (bacteria produce trimethylamine / TMA while breaking down proteins), which bacteria cause seafood spoilage (Pseudomonas, Shewanella), and how Morganella morganii produces histamine that causes scombroid poisoning. We then move to marine pharmacology — the marine drugs cytarabine (Ara-C) and vidarabine (Ara-A) from sponges, ziconotide — the powerful painkiller from the Conus magus cone snail venom, trabectedin from the sea squirt, and eribulin from the sponge Halichondria used in breast cancer treatment, plus omega-3 fatty acids.

Next: biofouling on ships — how microbes form biofilms and algae and barnacles settle, increasing drag and fuel consumption; the four types of corrosion (uniform, pitting, galvanic and microbially influenced corrosion / MIC); biofilm formation — reversible attachment, irreversible attachment, EPS matrix and maturation, dispersion — plus quorum sensing and dental plaque; and oceanography — physical, chemical, biological and geological branches, the epipelagic, mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones, and tools like CTD sensors, sonar mapping and satellites.

The video ends with practice questions based on the marine biotechnology csir net question pattern — pause the video and try them first, answers are explained right after. If this helped, please like, share and subscribe to Miss Biology. Watch Lecture 1 first if you missed it.

Description:

Titre: Cooling the Oceans with Smart Microalgae: A BioE3 Challenge Idea
Description:
Cooling the Oceans with Smart Microalgae: A BioE3 Challenge Idea
Can tiny ocean algae inspire a new way to reflect sunlight and capture carbon dioxide?
We present an innovative idea: “Cooling the Oceans with Smart Microalgae: Using Engineered Emiliania huxleyi to Fight Global Warming and Capture CO₂.”
Our idea explores whether a naturally occurring marine microalga, Emiliania huxleyi, could be developed into a biological approach for studying ocean reflectivity and carbon storage.
The Science Behind the Idea: The Albedo Effect
Emiliania huxleyi produces tiny white calcium carbonate plates called coccoliths. When these algae form dense blooms, their light-coloured appearance can influence how sunlight interacts with the ocean surface. The albedo effect describes the reflection of sunlight by a surface: brighter surfaces generally reflect more sunlight, while darker surfaces absorb more.
How Could We Explore This Idea?
As a proposed proof of concept, genetically modified strains designed to produce brighter, more reflective patches could be studied in laboratory tanks under controlled and contained conditions. Their performance could be compared with that of natural E. huxleyi strains.
Measurements could include:
a. Reflectivity and light absorption: to estimate whether the modified strains produce a measurable change in the reflection of incoming light.
b. Growth and coccolith production: to compare the brightness and biological characteristics of modified and natural strains.
c. CO₂ uptake and carbon balance: to measure carbon dioxide assimilation and assess how calcification affects the overall carbon balance.
d. Potential carbon export: to investigate whether any organic matter or calcium carbonate particles sink under the experimental conditions.
Importantly, CO₂ uptake during photosynthesis does not automatically mean long-term carbon sequestration. Calcification can also release CO₂, so the overall carbon balance and the fate of sinking material would need to be measured.
An Interesting Additional Factor: Coccolithoviruses
Natural viruses known as coccolithoviruses infect E. huxleyi and can influence the development and termination of its blooms. Research suggests that these interactions may also affect the release and sinking of carbon-containing particles. Understanding this natural relationship could be relevant to future research on bloom dynamics and ocean carbon cycling.

Safety Comes First
Any future research must prioritise the protection of marine ecosystems. Experiments would begin only in laboratory tanks under strict containment, with a proposed genetic safety switch designed to stop or limit the growth of the modified microalgae if unexpected harmful effects are detected. The switch would need to be rigorously tested, and additional safeguards would be essential because no genetic switch can be assumed to work perfectly. The aim is to explore this idea safely before considering any environmental application, protecting marine life must always come first.

Our Vision
This is an idea for scientific investigation, not a proven climate solution. By combining marine biology, biotechnology and the physics of sunlight, we hope to explore whether microalgae could offer useful insights into ocean reflectivity and carbon cycling.
Tiny algae. Big ideas. A brighter future.

Titre: They dive in a Saree, holding their breath to harvest seaweed in Rameshwaram
Description:
They dive underwater, hold their breath for up to 3 minutes, collect seaweed and surface only to empty it into the sack tied around their waist before diving back in.

These are the seaweed women of Rameswaram.
On Pamban Island in Tamil Nadu, women have dived for seaweed in the Gulf of Mannar for generations. Many start as young girls, learning the skill from the women before them.

Before every dive, they wrap each finger in strips of cloth to protect their hands from sharp rocks. Gloves slip off in strong currents, but cloth stays.

They also track the moon, which determines their harvesting calendar. They harvest for about 12 days a month, when the tides are gentler, leaving the reef alone in between so the seaweed can grow back.

But in 1986, the islands they worked on became part of the Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park, where collecting seaweed became illegal. The women responded by forming a union and taking steps to regulate their own harvest.

Today, dried seaweed fetches them around ₹110–115 a kilo. It eventually finds its way into products we use every day, from food to cosmetics. Yet the women who collect it rarely get to share in the value of the products their labour helps create.
India wants to grow its seaweed industry. But these women were in the water long before that ambition took shape.

Their knowledge, their labour and their future deserve to be part of that conversation.
Share this story to help the world hear the voices of Rameswaram’s seaweed women.

Titre: Biofloc Fish Farming: The $300/Ton Molasses Feed Trick
Description:
Biofloc fish farming uses $300/ton liquid molasses to turn toxic ammonia fish waste into 38% crude protein—cutting commercial tilapia feed bills by 10% or more.

In intensive aquaculture, feed accounts for over 40% of operating costs, yet fish excrete nearly 75% of feed nitrogen as gill-burning ammonia. By dosing carbohydrate-rich sugarcane molasses to raise the water's Carbon-to-Nitrogen (C/N) ratio to 12:1–15:1, heterotrophic bacteria rapidly lock up toxic ammonia (0.1 mg/L) and multiply into nutrient-dense biofloc clouds that tilapia graze on all day.

Across Colombia and the Caribbean—where imported pelleted feed can hit $75–$95 per bag—recycling waste nitrogen with local sugarcane byproducts is transforming commercial farm economics.

Titre: 🦐 Can Black Soldier Fly Meal Replace Fishmeal in Shrimp Feed?
Description:
Fishmeal is a common protein ingredient in shrimp feed. But could insect-based protein offer an alternative?

Researchers at ICAR-CIBA investigated this possibility using Black Soldier Fly (BSF) meal as a complete replacement for fishmeal in a shrimp feeding experiment lasting approximately 110 days, according to the institute’s 2025 Annual Report.

📊 What were the reported results?

🔹 Survival rate: 86% with BSF-based feed, compared with 70% in the control group.
🔹 Total production: 1,007 kg with BSF-based feed, compared with 907 kg in the control group.

The findings suggest that Black Soldier Fly meal could have potential as an alternative protein source for shrimp aquaculture feed.

However, these results reflect a specific experimental setup and do not guarantee the same performance on every shrimp farm.

Titre: SEARCA joins 22nd National Biotechnology Week (NBW) 2026 #searca
Description:
#SEARCA joined the 22nd National Biotechnology Week (NBW) 2026, held on 21-24 September 2026 at the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Quezon City. 

With the theme “Biotek para sa Kinabukasan: Kalikasan, Kalusugan, Kagandahan, Kabuhayan, at Kaunlaran,” it highlighted the role of biotechnology in advancing environmental sustainability, health, agriculture, livelihoods, and national development. 

The week-long event focused on agricultural biotechnology for climate-smart farming; environmental biotechnology for wastewater treatment and soil restoration; marine biotechnology for sustainable resource management; and biosafety education and workforce development. 

As a co-sponsor, SEARCA’s institutional exhibit showcased its Strengthening the Enabling Environment for the Development and Uptake of Modern Agricultural Biotechnology (SEED) Project, which aims to promote the responsible adoption of modern agricultural biotechnology in the Philippines, and its Bridging and Upgrading the Mechanisms and Pathways for the Uptake of Biotech (BUMP UP Biotech) Project, which aimed to identify pathways for the uptake of biotech innovations for food and nutrition security. Biotechnology-focused publications and institutional collaterals were also distributed at the booth. 

The Center’s participation in #NBW2026 underscores its commitment to advancing agricultural research and innovation, strengthening institutional capacities, and promoting knowledge and technology transfer.

Titre: Lessons from running a $250M healthtech & biotech fund, with Steve Burnell from Tenmile
Description:
Steve Burnell is managing director of Tenmile, the health technology and biotech investment business Andrew and Nicola Forrest's Tattarang set up with a 250 million dollar allocation. He is also a PhD marine ecologist who spent his twenties putting satellite trackers on right whales and making natural history documentaries, then spent fourteen years in big pharma, latterly running digital pathology and clinical decision support businesses for Roche.

He and Dr James Somauroo spend a long stretch on antimicrobial resistance, which Steve calls contrarian, and for good reason. Antibiotics have been the place capital goes to die, and big pharma has largely walked away. He explains why Tenmile went in anyway, across a vaccine company, a gram negative antibiotic and a point of care test that tells a GP whether an infection is bacterial or viral.

The most useful part for founders is on money. Steve is candid that he became a digital health sceptic after being the digital health guy in 1998, and he names a miss, Heidi Health, an Australian company Tenmile passed on. His line on it is "who looks like the idiot now".

There is also his advice on leadership, which starts from never having felt unworthy, why he thinks the best uses of AI in hospitals are the unglamorous ones, the regulatory absurdity of proving an algorithm against two pathologists who cannot agree with each other, and what Australia's R and D tax incentive is worth to a company on the register.

Titre: Sustainable Marine Biotechnology Explained Simply (11 Minutes)
Description:
In this video, we explore Sustainable Marine Biotechnology, an exciting field that combines biotechnology with the enormous biological diversity of oceans and marine ecosystems to develop products and solutions while protecting marine resources for future generations. Understanding sustainable marine biotechnology is important for students, researchers, biotechnology professionals, environmental scientists, and anyone interested in the future of the blue economy. We will cover the following key aspects:

Defining Sustainable Marine Biotechnology: Understanding how marine organisms, genes, enzymes, and biological processes can be used responsibly to create valuable products while minimizing environmental impact and conserving marine biodiversity.

Why Marine Biotechnology Matters: Exploring how oceans provide an enormous source of biological diversity that can contribute to healthcare, food production, renewable resources, environmental protection, and industrial innovation.

Marine Resources for Biotechnology: Examining important marine biological resources, including:

Marine Microorganisms: Exploring bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms that produce enzymes, metabolites, and other useful compounds.
Algae and Seaweeds: Understanding their applications in food, biofuels, biomaterials, cosmetics, and other sustainable products.
Marine Animals: Investigating organisms such as sponges, molluscs, corals, and other marine species as sources of bioactive compounds.
Marine Genetic Resources: Exploring how genomics, metagenomics, and biotechnology can help discover useful genes and biological pathways.

Sustainable Applications: Examining how marine biotechnology can contribute to sustainable solutions, including:

Sustainable Aquaculture: Developing improved feeds, disease management strategies, and breeding approaches while reducing environmental impacts.
Blue Bioeconomy: Creating valuable products from renewable marine resources and supporting new economic opportunities.
Marine Bioproducts: Developing biodegradable materials, enzymes, bioactive compounds, and other alternatives to petroleum-based products.
Environmental Biotechnology: Applying marine organisms and biological processes to pollution control, bioremediation, and ecosystem restoration.

Marine Biotechnology and Healthcare: Exploring how marine organisms can provide novel compounds for pharmaceuticals, nutraceuticals, and other health-related applications while considering responsible collection and production methods.

Balancing Innovation and Conservation: Understanding why marine biotechnology must balance scientific and commercial development with the protection of ecosystems, biodiversity, and vulnerable marine species.

Ethical and Environmental Considerations: Examining important issues such as bioprospecting, access to marine genetic resources, benefit sharing, intellectual property, habitat disturbance, and the potential ecological consequences of biotechnology activities.

The Role of Emerging Technologies: Exploring how artificial intelligence, marine genomics, synthetic biology, bioinformatics, and advanced cultivation techniques can improve the discovery and sustainable production of marine-derived products.

Future Trends: Highlighting emerging opportunities in marine carbon capture, sustainable aquaculture, algae-based products, marine biomaterials, blue biotechnology, ocean-based biorefineries, and ecosystem restoration.

By the end of this video, you will have a clear and comprehensive understanding of Sustainable Marine Biotechnology, including how marine biological resources can be transformed into innovative products and solutions while supporting conservation and long-term sustainability. Don’t miss the opportunity to discover how biotechnology can help us unlock the potential of the ocean without compromising the health of marine ecosystems!

Titre: Exploring Seaweed Polysaccharide Nanoparticles in Biotechnology-4K
Description:
The study asks a genuinely compelling question: do nanoparticles synthesized from sulfated polysaccharides (naturally derived from seaweed) inhibit the activity of microbes and cancer cells? It's a project that sits right at the intersection of marine biology, nanotechnology, and biomedical science.
 
 The research followed a rigorous experimental design:
 
 🔬 Extraction: Sulfated polysaccharides were isolated from seaweed through a multi-step solvent process (methanol, chloroform, and water) to remove fats and pigments, followed by boiling, filtration, and ethanol precipitation to yield the purified polysaccharide.
 
 🧪 Synthesis: The extracted polysaccharides were dissolved and combined with a metal solution, then sonicated until a visible color change confirmed nanoparticle formation, a green, biologically derived route to nanoparticle synthesis.
 
 🧫 Testing: The resulting nanoparticles were evaluated across bacterial strains, fungal strains, and cancer cell lines, examining antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer activity at varying concentrations.
 
 What stands out most is the scientific maturity behind the work: a clear hypothesis, carefully controlled variables (pH and temperature held constant while polysaccharide type and nanoparticle size were varied), and a testing protocol designed to validate the central question.
 
 Sustainable, marine-derived nanomedicine is a field with real promise, and it's inspiring to see that promise being explored by the next generation of scientists.

Titre: 80% of EU aquaculture comes from micro-producers | David Bassett
Description:
80% of aquaculture production in the European Union comes from micro-producers: organisations of ten employees or fewer.

David Bassett is General Secretary of EATIP, the European Aquaculture Technology and Innovation Platform, and vice-chair for the aquatic sector of the Working Group on Primary Producers of the Circular Bio-based Europe Joint Undertaking (CBE JU). In this interview, he explains why aquaculture is still misheard as agriculture, how the artisanal and family scale of Europe's fish, shellfish and algae farmers limits their capacity to engage in research and innovation, and what the aquatic sector can learn from the knowledge transfer systems built for land-based agriculture.

Titre: How are Salmon Raised in Recirculating Aquaculture Systems?
Chaîne: UW-Stevens Point Northern Aquaculture Demonstration Facility
Description:
Currently, around 95% of salmon consumed in the US are imported, contributing $3.4 billion annually to the country's trade deficit. Most of the world's farmed salmon are grown in floating coastal net pens, which may introduce risk from external factors such as severe weather and pathogens. Use of net pens in the United States is also constrained by regulations. This video explains how salmon can be raised in indoor recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS), which can produce salmon locally on land using sustainable practices to manage effluent, biosecurity, and water use. 
This video is part of a 17-objective project called Sustainable Aquaculture Systems: Supporting Atlantic Salmon (SAS2) funded by the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture. Learn more at: https://salmononland.org/

Titre: Appel à don pour enquêter sur les micro-algues génétiquement modifiées
Chaîne: Inf'OGM - Veille citoyenne sur les OGM, les semences et les biotechnologies
Description:
En Europe, les micro-organismes génétiquement modifiés (MGM) pourraient bientôt être présents en tant que tel dans l'alimentation, les cosmétiques, et disséminer dans l'environnement pour des usages agricoles. Pourtant, leurs impacts sur les écosytèmes ou la santé restent largement méconnus. En revanche, il est d’ores et déjà certain que ces micro-organismes seront brevetés, engendrant une insécurité juridique et une privatisation du vivant.

Page de don sur Hello Asso : https://www.helloasso.com/associations/inf-ogm/collectes/1-for-the-planet-double-votre-don-2026

Pour permettre un véritable débat démocratique, une information indépendante est indispensable.

Le 17 juin 2026, l’Union européenne a déréglementé la mise sur le marché des OGM, rebaptisés NTG. Cette déréglementation concerne les végétaux y compris les micro-algues. Mais, la veille, le 16 juin, les États membres de l’UE se sont aussi accordés sur un texte visant à quasiment déréglementer la commercialisation et la dissémination dans l'environnement des micro-organismes GM (MGM). Ce texte propose de supprimer l'évaluation des risques, l’étiquetage, et le suivi post-commercial.

Inf’OGM souhaite faire la lumière sur les projets de modification génétique des micro-organismes - virus, bactérie, champignon, levure -, leurs impacts environnementaux et sanitaires ainsi que les enjeux politiques associés. Cette enquête inclura également les micro-algues.

L’ enquête visera à produire un état des lieux actuel de la recherche, des exemples de développements industriels en cours, des exemples de perspectives de commercialisation, ainsi que sur les acteurs et organisations impliqués. Une attention particulière sera accordée à la traçabilité, aux risques de dissémination dans la nature et à la privatisation du vivant par le biais des brevets.

Ainsi, par exemple, l'Australie a autorisé la dissémination dans l'environnement d’une souche génétiquement modifiée de la micro-algue marine Nannochloropsis oceanica, conçue pour la production accrue d’acides gras (lipides) pour des usages industriels (nutrition, cosmétique, éventuellement biocarburants).

Titre: Australian Aquaculture Episode 4 🐟
Description:
Australian Aquaculture Ep. 4 🇦🇺

This… is Western Australia. The Oz I grew up seeing on postcards and TV. And in Broome, barramundi is king.

We’re at the start of the journey, inside Tassal’s barramundi nursery helping shape the future of one of Australia’s most iconic fish. These fingerlings don’t all start here. They’re brought in from Victoria, making a long journey north before entering a tightly controlled nursery system rebuilt on recirculating aquaculture technology.

Why so much care? Because this is where future generations will be defined. Selective breeding programs are just getting underway here, selecting for traits like heat tolerance, growth efficiency, and disease resistance.

But first, you have to get them through the nursery stage. And barramundi don’t make it easy. They’re cannibalistic by nature, which means grading – separating fish by size – is one of the most important jobs here. Four months later, those carefully raised juveniles are ready for the sea.

Next stop: Cone Bay.

Where the outback meets the ocean.
