Future of Biotech: 9.4_Cultivated Seafood #biotechnology #ai #seafood #shorts
Description:
What if we could enjoy salmon, tuna, shrimp, crab, and lobster without overfishing the oceans or harming marine ecosystems? Cultivated seafood uses cellular agriculture to grow real seafood directly from a small sample of fish or shellfish cells, eliminating the need to catch or farm entire animals. By combining stem cell biology, tissue engineering, bioprinting, precision fermentation, synthetic biology, and artificial intelligence, scientists are producing authentic seafood with the same cellular composition, taste, and nutrition while reducing pressure on wild fish populations. As global seafood demand continues to rise, cultivated seafood offers a promising solution to improve food security while protecting marine biodiversity and creating a more sustainable blue economy.

The production process begins with a small biopsy of muscle or stem cells from a healthy fish or shellfish. These cells are expanded in nutrient-rich cell culture media, guided to differentiate into muscle and fat tissues, and grown on edible scaffolds or through 3D bioprinting to recreate the texture of conventional seafood. Researchers are developing cultivated salmon, tuna, shrimp, eel, crab, lobster, octopus, squid, and caviar, while advancing serum-free growth media, AI-optimized bioreactors, edible biomaterials, CRISPR-assisted cell engineering, and precision fermentation to improve scalability, reduce production costs, and enhance nutritional value. Cultivated seafood also avoids common concerns such as microplastics, mercury accumulation, parasites, antibiotics, and overexploitation of marine species.

The future of cultivated seafood extends beyond replacing conventional fishing—it could fundamentally reshape how humanity sources protein from the oceans. Scientists envision carbon-neutral seafood production, personalized nutrition, omega-3-enhanced fish, hybrid plant-cell seafood, offshore biomanufacturing, and even food production for lunar and Martian habitats. While challenges remain in scaling manufacturing, reducing costs, achieving regulatory approval, and gaining consumer acceptance, cultivated seafood represents one of the most exciting frontiers in food biotechnology. By producing real seafood without depleting marine ecosystems, it has the potential to protect ocean biodiversity while ensuring a reliable supply of nutritious protein for generations to come.

Titre: Class 10th Chapter No.08 Biotechnology Lecture No.07 Environmental and Marine Biotechnology
Core Technologies: 2.1_Color Codes of Biotechnology #biotechnology #science
Description:
Biotechnology is far more diverse than genetic engineering alone. To organize its rapidly expanding applications across medicine, agriculture, industry, environmental science, marine biology, computing, ethics, and national security, scientists use a globally recognized color-coding system. In this episode, explore the fascinating world of the Color Codes of Biotechnology and discover how each color represents a unique field that is transforming science, healthcare, food production, sustainability, and the future of humanity.

Learn why biotechnology has evolved into one of the most interdisciplinary sciences ever created, bringing together biology, chemistry, genetics, engineering, computer science, medicine, artificial intelligence, nanotechnology, and environmental science. Understand how the color classification helps researchers, educators, policymakers, and industries organize innovations that span from curing diseases to protecting ecosystems and even enabling space exploration.

Discover Red Biotechnology, the branch dedicated to human and veterinary medicine. Explore breakthroughs in gene therapy, CRISPR gene editing, stem cell therapy, regenerative medicine, tissue engineering, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, mRNA technology, precision medicine, diagnostics, pharmacogenomics, immunotherapy, organ transplantation, and personalized healthcare that are revolutionizing modern medicine.

Journey into Green Biotechnology, where genetics and plant science are improving agriculture through genetically modified crops, genome editing, biofertilizers, biopesticides, drought-resistant plants, climate-resilient agriculture, crop improvement, sustainable farming, vertical farming, and food security for a growing global population.

Explore White Biotechnology, the industrial powerhouse that uses microorganisms, enzymes, fermentation, and synthetic biology to manufacture biofuels, biodegradable plastics, industrial enzymes, pharmaceuticals, sustainable chemicals, bio-based materials, renewable energy, and eco-friendly manufacturing processes, reducing dependence on fossil fuels and minimizing environmental impact.

Dive beneath the oceans with Blue Biotechnology, which harnesses marine organisms to develop novel medicines, marine enzymes, bioactive compounds, aquaculture innovations, biomaterials, nutraceuticals, and marine conservation technologies while unlocking the enormous biological potential hidden within Earth's oceans.

Discover Grey Biotechnology, focused on protecting the environment through bioremediation, wastewater treatment, pollution control, waste recycling, carbon capture, ecological restoration, biodiversity conservation, microbial cleanup, and sustainable environmental management, helping restore ecosystems damaged by human activity.

Learn about Yellow Biotechnology, centered on food science, nutrition, fermentation, probiotics, functional foods, food preservation, brewing, dairy technology, and nutritional biotechnology, improving both the quality and safety of the foods we consume every day.

Explore Gold Biotechnology, where biology meets computation through bioinformatics, computational biology, artificial intelligence, systems biology, genomics, big data, machine learning, molecular modeling, and digital biotechnology, enabling scientists to analyze massive biological datasets and accelerate scientific discovery.

Understand the growing importance of Brown Biotechnology, which develops solutions for desert ecosystems, arid-land agriculture, drought-resistant organisms, water conservation, and sustainable development in harsh environments, supporting life in some of Earth's most challenging climates.

Discover Purple Biotechnology, the field addressing the ethical, legal, regulatory, intellectual property, biosafety, biosecurity, and societal implications of biotechnology, ensuring scientific innovation is developed responsibly and ethically.

Explore Black Biotechnology, focused on biodefense, forensic biotechnology, pathogen detection, biosecurity, infectious disease preparedness, biodefense research, and preventing the misuse of biotechnology, safeguarding public health and national security.

Meet the emerging fields of Orange Biotechnology, dedicated to science communication, biotechnology education, public engagement, outreach, and scientific literacy, helping bridge the gap between researchers and society, as well as Violet Biotechnology, which integrates law, governance, policy, and international regulation for responsible innovation. Discover additional specialized branches including Silver Biotechnology (aging and longevity), Dark Biotechnology (extremophiles and deep biosphere research), and Rainbow Biotechnology, representing the convergence of multiple biotechnology disciplines.

Titre: Webinaire - Stratégie régionale pour le développement de la Biotechnologie bleue dans l’océan Indien
Description:
Face aux défis croissants liés au changement climatique et à la pression exercée sur les ressources marines, la biotechnologie bleue s’impose comme un levier stratégique pour concilier innovation, développement économique durable et préservation des écosystèmes. Malgré un potentiel considérable dans la région, les initiatives demeurent encore fragmentées et les synergies régionales insuffisamment développées.

Avec cette étude « Stratégie régionale pour le développement de la biotechnologie bleue dans les îles de l’océan Indien », menée avec l’appui de l’Agence française de développement, Cap Business Océan Indien entend soutenir l’émergence et la structuration de cette filière d’avenir. Depuis septembre 2025, ce travail a été piloté par le groupe Cofrepeche–Creocéan, mobilisant les acteurs publics, privés, scientifiques et institutionnels des six territoires de l’Indianocéanie.

A travers ce webinaire de restitution, les experts présenteront les principales conclusions de leur étude, en particulier les opportunités, les défis et les actions prioritaires nécessaires à la structuration d’un écosystème régional innovant, compétitif et durable. Titre: #akuakultur
Description:
Budidaya Ikan Tuna Sirip Biru


Source :
1.🎥@sladeit


Siapa sangka, ikan kecil yang terlihat seperti dibuang ini, justru menjadi santapan termahal bagi tuna sirip biru bernilai miliaran rupiah. Di Port Lincoln Australia Selatan, para peternak memiliki cara unik untuk memberi makan tuna sirip biru. Ribuan ikan umpan tidak dilempar langsung ke dalam keramba, melainkan dimasukkan ke sebuah mesin berputar berkecepatan tinggi. Saat mesin bekerja, ikan-ikan kecil itu langsung dicacah dan disebarkan ke seluruh penjuru keramba menggunakan gaya sentrifugal. Hasilnya pakan tersebar merata tanpa menumpuk di satu titik. Metode ini membuat setiap tuna memiliki kesempatan makan yang sama. Tuna yang lebih besar tidak bisa menguasai seluruh makanan, sementara tuna yang lebih kecil tetap mendapatkan bagian. Seluruh kawanan pun harus terus berenang sambil mencari pakan, sehingga pertumbuhan mereka menjadi lebih merata. Selain meningkatkan efisiensi, cara ini juga mengurangi pakan yang tenggelam ke dasar laut, sehingga limbah berkurang dan kualitas air tetap terjaga. Setelah melalui proses penggemukan selama 3 hingga 7 bulan, tuna-tuna ini berkembang menjadi tuna sirip biru premium dengan daging padat dan marbling lemak yang sempurna, menjadikannya salah satu bahan sashimi paling mahal di dunia.

Titre: la pisciculture  c'est une activité durable et rentable
Plantes et microalgues contre les métaux lourds 🌿🌱- Festival de vulgarisation Pint of Science
Description:
Intervention filmée à l'occasion du festival de vulgarisation scientifique Pint of Science

- La phytoremédiation au secours de l’environnement
Stéphane Ravanel (Directeur de recherche - Laboratoire Physiologie Cellulaire & Végétale - CEA-CNRS-UGA – INRAE) - https://www.lpcv.fr/Pages/MetalStress/Presentation.aspx 

La phytoremédiation est un procédé durable qui utilise les plantes et les microalgues pour dépolluer des écosystèmes contaminés par des métaux lourds. Nous analyserons comment ces organismes se comportent dans des sols et eaux contaminés et décrirons les propriétés exceptionnelles de certaines espèces, leur tolérance (survivre malgré la toxicité) et leur capacité d’accumulation (aptitude à stocker les métaux). Nous verrons ensuite comment ces capacités sont mises à profit à travers différentes approches, comme la phytostabilisation ou la phytoextraction, pour restaurer des sites pollués.

- Les secrets moléculaires de ces dépollueurs
Jonathan Przybyla-Toscano (Chargé de recherche - Laboratoire Physiologie Cellulaire & Végétale - CEA-CNRS-UGA – INRAE) - 

Comment certaines plantes et microalgues parviennent-elles à tolérer et à accumuler massivement les métaux lourds ? Grâce à un arsenal moléculaire sophistiqué qui agit à trois niveaux : un prélèvement renforcé, un transport efficace vers les parties aériennes dans le cas des plantes, et une séquestration dans des territoires cellulaires spécialisés qui protègent la machinerie biologique. Nous plongerons dans la génétique de ces organismes pour identifier les gènes et protéines clés derrière cette tolérance et accumulation exceptionnelles.

Titre: PANEL - FINANCE DE TRANSITION EN ACTION : ENSEIGNEMENTS CLÉS DE L'ÉCONOMIE BLEUE
Description:
Les infrastructures côtières, le transport maritime, les systèmes portuaires et les écosystèmes marins illustrent la complexité de la transition dans des secteurs simultanément exposés à l'accélération des risques climatiques physiques et à une forte interdépendance économique mondiale. À partir de l'économie bleue comme terrain d'analyse concret, cette session explore comment l'allocation du capital, les contraintes opérationnelles et la planification des infrastructures doivent s'articuler pour permettre une décarbonation crédible, tout en préservant la résilience et la compétitivité. Comment les institutions financières, les opérateurs portuaires et les entreprises de transport maritime peuvent-ils mieux aligner les horizons d'investissement avec les réalités opérationnelles de systèmes maritimes fortement capitalistiques ? Qu'est-ce qui distingue des trajectoires de transition crédibles dans les ports et le transport maritime d'ajustements marginaux qui prolongent les vulnérabilités structurelles ? Comment les opérateurs privés, les investisseurs et les autorités publiques peuvent-ils mieux partager la responsabilité d'assurer à la fois la continuité des échanges, la sécurité énergétique et la résilience climatique à long terme ?

Romina Reversi, Directrice générale, Responsable de la Banque d'investissement durable, Amériques, Crédit Agricole - CIB

PANEL - TRANSITION FINANCE IN PRACTICE : LESSONS FROM THE BLUE ECONOMY

Coastal infrastructure, maritime transport, port systems, and marine ecosystems illustrate the complexity of managing transition in sectors exposed simultaneously to accelerating physical climate risks and deep global economic interdependence. Using the blue economy as a real-world lens, this session examines how capital allocation, operational constraints, and infrastructure planning must align to deliver credible decarbonization while preserving resilience and competitiveness. How can financial institutions, port operators, and freight companies better align investment timelines with operational realities in capital-intensive maritime systems? What distinguishes credible transition pathways in ports and shipping from incremental adjustments that risk prolonging structural exposure? How should private operators, investors, and public authorities share responsibility for balancing trade continuity, energy security, and long-term climate resilience?

Titre: How Machine Learning is Transforming Marine Biotechnology 🌊🤖
Description:
Welcome to this deep dive into our latest research published in Frontiers in Plant Science (2024), titled: "Machine learning-based prediction models unleash the enhanced production of fucoxanthin in Isochrysis galbana."

Manochkumar J, Jonnalagadda A, Cherukuri AK, Vannier B, Janjaroen D, Chandrasekaran R and Ramamoorthy S (2024) Machine learning-based prediction models unleash the enhanced production of fucoxanthin in Isochrysis galbana. Front. Plant Sci. 15:1461610. doi: 10.3389/fpls.2024.1461610


🔬 About the Research:
Fucoxanthin is a high-value marine carotenoid (xanthophyll) found abundantly in the microalga Isochrysis galbana. It has immense global market potential with widespread applications across the food, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical, and cosmetic industries. However, conventional methods for optimizing and quantifying its production are highly time-consuming, expensive, and logistically complex.
To solve this, our study introduced an integrated experimental framework paired with advanced Machine Learning (ML) predictive modeling. By altering the types and concentrations of phytohormone supplementations, we evaluated how data-driven insights can streamline microalgae cultivation.

🔗 Read the full open-access paper here: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/plant-science/articles/10.3389/fpls.2024.1461610/full

Titre: Establishing public-private partnerships? Examples in blue biotechnology (Interreg Euro-MED Academy)
Description:
The marine (blue) biotechnology sector can have a significant impact on the environment, human wellbeing and economic growth, however in the Mediterranean basin it is currently in its infancy. Hence, the creation of innovation communities is of high priority to advance in this field. The 2B-BLUE project (supported by Interreg Euro-MED) supports the creation of blue biotechnology networks accross the Mediterranean. Six countries (Albania, France, Greece, Italy, Slovenia and Spain) reppresenting the project piloted the blue biotechnology value chains by creating public-private partnerships to test and develop new technologies. 

This video shows how to create such partnerships and how to replicate our good practices. We present these case studies:
1. Albania: innovative integrated multitrophic aquaculture systems (fish, mussels, pearl oysters and sea cucumbers)
2. France: microalgae cultivation for food and other industries
3. Greece: a) integrated sea cucumber and mussel farming, b) floating microalgae cultivation
4. Slovenia: a) microalgae cultivation, b) integrated sea cucumber and mussel farming, c) valorization of marine biomass
5. Spain: bioremediation through algae cultivation

The video is a part of 2B-BLUE (Boosting the Blue Biotechnology community in the Mediterranean) Interreg Euro-MED project, co-financed by the European Union.

Titre: Moroni accueille une table ronde clé sur la biotechnologie bleue dans l’océan Indien
Description:
HaYba ECONOMIE
La Biotechnologie Bleue au Cœur d'une Table Ronde Régionale à la Chambre de Commerce de  Moroni

Cap Business Océan Indien, en partenariat avec la Chambre de Commerce, d'Industrie et d'Agriculture de Ngazidja, organise ce jeudi 30 avril une table ronde multi-acteurs consacrée au développement de la biotechnologie bleue dans la région de l'océan Indien.

La rencontre, prévue à partir de 08h00 à la salle de conférence de la CCIA Ngazidja (Moroni Port), réunit des acteurs de haut niveau autour d'un secteur stratégique encore largement sous-exploité dans l'archipel et dans l'ensemble de la zone.

La biotechnologie bleue désigne l'ensemble des applications issues de la recherche sur les ressources biologiques marines,algues, organismes marins, micro-organismes côtiers, dont le potentiel couvre des domaines aussi variés que la pharmacologie, l'agroalimentaire, les biocarburants ou encore la cosmétique. 
Pour un pays comme les Comores, dont l'espace maritime représente un atout considérable, le développement de cette filière constitue un enjeu de souveraineté économique autant que de diversification productive.
La tenue de cet événement aux Comores témoigne de la volonté de positionner le pays comme partie prenante des dynamiques économiques régionales, dans un contexte où plusieurs pays de l'océan Indien cherchent à valoriser leurs ressources marines au-delà de la pêche traditionnelle.

Titre: Types of Biotechnology | Did You Know Biotechnology Comes in Colors?
Description:
Do you know the colors of Biotechnology?

 Biotechnology is a broad field, and to make it easier to understand, scientists group it into different types using colors. Each color represents how biotechnology is applied in real life. In this video, we will explain the major types of biotechnology in simple terms and why each one is important.

Let’s start with Red Biotechnology.
Red biotechnology focuses on medicine and healthcare. This type of biotechnology is used to develop vaccines, antibiotics, insulin, and other life-saving drugs. It also plays a major role in medical research, disease diagnosis, and gene therapy. For example, the production of vaccines and the use of biotechnology to treat diseases like diabetes and cancer fall under red biotechnology. Its main goal is to improve human health and save lives.

Next is Green Biotechnology.
Green biotechnology is applied in agriculture and food production. It helps scientists develop improved crops that grow faster, resist diseases, tolerate drought, and produce higher yields. Farmers benefit from green biotechnology through genetically improved crops that reduce the need for pesticides and increase food security. Examples include disease-resistant maize, improved rice varieties, and crops that can grow in harsh environmental conditions. Green biotechnology plays a key role in feeding the world’s growing population.

The third type is White Biotechnology, also known as industrial biotechnology.
This type focuses on using living organisms, such as bacteria and enzymes, in industrial processes. White biotechnology helps industries produce goods in a cleaner and more environmentally friendly way. It is used in the production of biofuels, biodegradable plastics, detergents, and chemicals. Compared to traditional industrial methods, white biotechnology reduces pollution, saves energy, and promotes sustainable manufacturing.

Another important type is Blue Biotechnology.
Blue biotechnology involves the use of marine and aquatic organisms found in oceans, seas, and freshwater environments. Scientists study marine plants, algae, and microorganisms to develop medicines, cosmetics, and industrial products. For example, some drugs used to treat cancer and infections are derived from marine organisms. Blue biotechnology also supports environmental conservation and sustainable use of marine resources.

In summary, biotechnology may be one science, but it has many applications.
Red biotechnology improves healthcare, green biotechnology supports agriculture, white biotechnology enhances industrial production, and blue biotechnology explores the potential of marine life. Together, these types of biotechnology help solve real-world problems and improve the quality of life.

Understanding these types helps us appreciate how biotechnology contributes to health, food security, industry, and environmental sustainability.

Cette capsule vous plonge au cœur d’un projet mené en partenariat avec une entreprise maricole québécoise, où la co‑culture en mer de macroalgues et de moules bleues est explorée comme avenue prometteuse pour renforcer la résilience des fermes aquacoles face aux changements climatiques. Valentin Cavarlé, étudiant au doctorat à l’UQAR–ISMER, nous présente ses travaux réalisés sous la direction de Fanny Noisette (UQAR–ISMER), Éric Tamigneaux (EPAQ–Cégep), Réjean Tremblay (UQAR–ISMER) et Fabrice Pernet (IFREMER, Plouzané). Il tente de démontrer comment ces deux espèces peuvent se soutenir mutuellement afin d’offrir aux producteurs des pistes concrètes pour une aquaculture plus durable et mieux adaptée aux réalités côtières du Québec.

Les fermes aquacoles côtières font face à des pressions croissantes liées aux changements climatiques et à la fragilisation des écosystèmes marins. Au Québec, les petites exploitations sont particulièrement concernées, mais elles offrent aussi un cadre idéal pour tester des pratiques innovantes. Mon projet de recherche porte sur la co-culture en mer de la macroalgue Saccharina latissima et de la moule bleue Mytilus edulis, un modèle encore peu développé au Québec.
La co-culture repose sur une idée simple : associer des espèces différentes pour qu’elles se bénéficient mutuellement. Les algues peuvent capter une partie des rejets produits par les mollusques et produire de la matière organique qui peut contribuer à leur alimentation. Cette interaction pourrait à la fois réduire l’impact environnemental des fermes et améliorer la croissance et la qualité des moules.
À partir de suivis réalisés directement en mer, ce projet cherche à mieux comprendre les avantages concrets de la co-culture algue-mollusque pour les fermes marines. L’objectif est de produire des connaissances utiles aux producteurs et de proposer des pistes pour une aquaculture plus résiliente, mieux adaptée aux réalités des côtes québécoises.

Ce projet est soutenu par le Fonds d’excellence en recherche Apogée Canada (CFREF – Transforming Climate Action), par les Fonds de recherche du Québec à travers le programme Projets Nouvelle Équipe – Pôle Bioalimentaire 2024 2025, ainsi que par une bourse d’excellence de l’ISMER pour le doctorat en océanographie et Ressources Aquatiques Québec (RAQ). 
Il s’insère pleinement dans l’axe « Aquaculture » de la programmation scientifique du RAQ, en contribuant autant à l’avancement des connaissances fondamentales sur les interactions macroalgues bivalves qu’au développement de systèmes de production plus efficaces et résilients. En documentant les bénéfices de la co culture sur l’autosuffisance alimentaire, la performance des organismes et l’intégration des niveaux trophiques, ce projet offre des pistes concrètes pour soutenir une aquaculture durable et adaptée aux réalités des petites exploitations maricoles du Québec.

Le RAQ est supporté financièrement depuis 2006 par le Fonds de recherche du Québec - Nature et technologies (Programme regroupements stratégiques).

Titre: Planète conférences - Biodiversité marine et biomimétisme
Description:
Biodiversité marine et biomimétisme, quand le vivant nous inspire

Conférence de Nadia Améziane, Professeure au Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle Station marine de Concarneau.

Les océans représentent plus de 90% du volume habitable de notre planète et abritent entre 13% à 15% de la biodiversité mondiale avec 230 000 à 275 000 espèces décrites. Les scientifiques estiment qu'au moins 50 % et, potentiellement, plus de 90 % des espèces marines reste à découvrir. La biodiversité marine est à l’origine de nombreuses découvertes majeures pour la compréhension des systèmes biologiques. Elle a un impact important pour l’humanité, notamment, en : régulant le climat ; protégeant les rivages de l’érosion grâce aux organismes bio-constructeurs ou aux végétaux : fournissant la principale source de protéines à plus de 17 % de la population mondiale, produisant de l’oxygène ; etc. La biodiversité marine quel que soit l’échelle, depuis la molécule jusqu’à l’écosystème en passant par la biologie des organismes ou leur éthologie, est source d’inspiration pour élaborer des éco-innovations au monde socio-économique dans de nombreux domaines tels que, par exemple, le design, l’architecture, l’industrie, la cosmétique, la médecine. Attention, cependant, à être vigilants car la biodiversité est fragile et fortement impactée par le changement global. Veillons à ne pas rentrer dans une démarche utilitariste de la biodiversité et contribuons à sauvegarder le potentiel évolutif du vivant.

Our oceans are emptying. Over 90% of the world's fish stocks are either fully exploited or dangerously depleted. Industrial fishing is facing a systemic collapse. But what if we could grow the perfect fillet of tuna or salmon... in a bioreactor?

In this episode of Star_Mind, we dive deep into the revolutionary technology of cellular aquaculture. This isn't science fiction; it's a present-day reality being developed by companies like BlueNalu and leading researchers at the University of California.

We explore how real fish meat is cultivated directly from cells, the profound advantages it offers (zero mercury, zero microplastics), and the fundamental challenges the industry must overcome: from taste tests and regulatory approvals to the immense problem of scaling production.

Is this the dawn of a new era in human nutrition? And can we save our oceans by finally stop fishing in them?

Titre: Today's World of Biotechnology | Types of Biotechnology Explained (Red, White, Green & Blue)
Description:
Biotechnology is a multidisciplinary field that blends natural sciences and engineering to create innovations in medicine, agriculture, marine science, and industries.
In this video, we discuss the four major types of biotechnology with simple examples:

🔬 Red Biotechnology – Related to medicine, including vaccines, medicines, and diagnostic tools.
🏭 White Biotechnology – Industrial biotechnology focused on enzymes, biofuels, and eco-friendly production.
🌱 Green Biotechnology – Agricultural biotechnology that improves crops, yield, and nutritional value.
🌊 Blue Biotechnology – Marine biotechnology involving aquatic organisms and marine-based products.

📌 Also learn about the Father of Biotechnology: Karoly Ereky, who coined the term in 1919.

Titre: Tester les microalgues comme appâts pour la pêche aux crustacés
Description:
Les populations de poissons pélagiques tels que le maquereau et le hareng, traditionnellement utilisés comme appâts pour la pêche de crustacés au Québec, sont en déclin et font l’objet d’un moratoire en mer canadienne depuis 2021.  

Une équipe du Biodôme, dirigée par le Dre Nathalie R. Le François, et ses partenaires académiques, industriels et en biotechnologies examinent la possibilité d’utiliser une base de microalgues comme solution écoresponsable pour remplacer l’appât traditionnel.   

Dans cette vidéo, découvrez les premières expérimentations de pêche à l’oursin vert menées avec la Première Nation Wolastoqiyik Wahsipekuk au large de Cacouna. 

Le financement de ces activités est assuré par la Fondation Espace pour la vie, la Première Nation Wolastoqiyik Wahsipekuk et l’Université Laval.

Invisibles à l’œil nu mais omniprésentes, les microalgues jouent un rôle essentiel dans le fonctionnement des écosystèmes aquatiques. Ces organismes unicellulaires, capables de photosynthèse, produisent une part importante de l’oxygène que nous respirons, stockent du carbone, et forment la base de la chaîne alimentaire dans les océans. Leur incroyable diversité – de formes, de couleurs, de modes de vie – et leur capacité à s’adapter à des milieux extrêmes, des eaux polaires aux sources thermales, les rendent aussi fascinantes qu’indispensables. Mais les microalgues ne sont pas seulement utiles dans la nature. Certaines espèces sont cultivées pour leurs propriétés nutritionnelles, cosmétiques ou thérapeutiques, et suscitent un vif intérêt en recherche et en innovation. De la culture en laboratoire à l’extraction de molécules d’intérêt, cette conférence abordera les techniques et les défis liés à leur valorisation, avec un focus sur les travaux menés en Nouvelle-Calédonie par l’Ifremer et la Technopole. Toutefois, toutes ne sont pas aussi bienveillantes, une grosse centaine d’espèces sont connues pour être toxiques ou nuisibles - marées rouges, contamination de poissons et de fruits de mer, notamment par les ciguatoxines responsables de la gratte dans le Pacifique. Ces microalgues toxiques ont des impacts majeurs sur la biodiversité, la santé humaine, et les activités économiques. Cette conférence abordera les études menées dans ce domaine en Nouvelle-Calédonie. À travers une approche accessible et vulgarisée, cette conférence vous invite à découvrir ce monde microscopique, entre espoir biotechnologique et menace écologique, et à mieux comprendre les enjeux qu’il représente à l’heure du changement global.

Blue Biotechnology - Blue biotechnology is the branch of biotechnology that explores and utilizes marine and freshwater resources—such as organisms, plants, and microbes—for industrial, medical, agricultural, and environmental applications.
Core Focus:
It harnesses the unique biochemical compounds and adaptations found in aquatic life forms to develop innovative products and solutions.
Key Applications:
    Pharmaceuticals:
        Development of new drugs from marine organisms (e.g., anti-cancer agents from sponges).
    Enzymes & Industrial Products:
        Heat- and salt-resistant enzymes from deep-sea microbes for food, textile, and biofuel industries.
    Cosmetics:
        Anti-aging and UV-protection compounds from algae and marine bacteria.
    Aquaculture:
        Genetic improvement of fish and shellfish, sustainable feed production, and disease-resistant strains.
    Environmental:
        Bioremediation of oil spills and heavy metals using marine microorganisms.
Importance:
    Biodiversity treasure: Oceans hold more than 80% of the planet’s biodiversity.
    Novel compounds: Many marine species produce chemicals not found in terrestrial organisms.
    Sustainability: Offers eco-friendly solutions for health, food, and industry.

On parle aussi des défis techniques en milieu nordique, de l’évolution du marché des algues au Québec, et de la manière dont ce super-aliment s’intègre peu à peu dans la culture culinaire locale.

Comment préserver les écosystèmes tout en développant un secteur économique durable?
Quelle vision pour l’avenir de la mariculture dans le Saint-Laurent?
Un échange riche sur l’innovation bleue, l’alimentation de demain et le rêve d’un fleuve nourricier et respecté.

Titre: Toux et troubles respiratoires liés à des micro algues, lors de baignades.
Description:
La prolifération de micro algues dans l'eau peut générer des troubles respiratoires après une baignade.
Ostréopsis est une micro algue, appartenant au plancton, qui est capable de proliférer lorsque la température de l'eau est supérieure à 20°C.
Elle sécrète une toxine qui est responsable de troubles respiratoires, surtout la toux, lorsque elle est abondante dans l'eau des plages. Sa présence est surveillée, et peut conduire à fermer momentanément les plages si elle est trop abondante.
La prolifération de vette algue semble bien liée au réchauffement climatique.

Titre: Harnessing Biotech. for a Greener Africa: Prof. Onwurah Ikechukwu’s Vision for Decarbonization
Description:
At the World Decarbonization Day (WDD) 2024, Professor Onwurah Ikechukwu, a renowned Professor of Biochemistry and Environmental Biotechnology Consultant from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka delivered a forward-thinking presentation on a topic of global urgency:
“Integrating Industrial and Environmental Biotechnology for Decarbonisation—with Opportunities for Africa.”

Following an inspiring presentation by children from the OLOGEDI Energy Club, Prof. Ikechukwu took the stage to share groundbreaking research and innovations born from African laboratories—with the potential to transform how the world reduces carbon emissions.

🔬 Reimagining Carbon Reduction Through Microorganisms
Professor Ikechukwu began by redefining decarbonization—not just as a climate obligation, but as a technological opportunity. He introduced industrial biotechnology as a key strategy, specifically spotlighting the role of engineered microorganisms in producing eco-friendly industrial substances and minimizing carbon emissions.

One of his central innovations was a tailored microbial consortium—a combination of microorganisms designed to work in harmony to break down waste and generate useful products. In one successful case, Prof. Ikechukwu’s team used banana peels to produce nano bioethanol, a clean energy source that also cuts down on energy costs during production.

🌊 Bioremediation for Oil Industry Waste
Turning to environmental applications, he explained how his team tackled marine pollution caused by animal waste from oil operations. Using a biochemical dynamics process, they significantly reduced toxicity and carbon emissions, with tested carbon dioxide output as low as 0.05 tons—an impressive outcome demonstrating biotechnology’s power to reverse environmental damage.

💡 Biosurfactants: Africa’s Untapped Goldmine
A highlight of the presentation was his work on biosurfactants—biodegradable, non-toxic agents traditionally used in the petroleum industry to enhance oil recovery and clean up hydrocarbon spills. These agents, typically made through chemical synthesis, were produced in Prof. Ikechukwu’s lab using a microbial blend of Pseudomonas spp. and Azotobacter.

Pseudomonas produces biosurfactants.

Azotobacter captures nitrogen from the air, reducing external inputs and enhancing sustainability.

Though the production yield per liter was modest, the low energy requirement and high market value made it both scalable and economically viable, especially for African countries rich in organic waste like rice husks and banana peels.

🌍 A Sustainable Future for Africa
Prof. Ikechukwu concluded with a bold vision:

Titre: Dr. Cathy Walsh: Cell cultures with seafood relevant marine species
Description:
Seminar Series: The Science of Alt. Protein
Cell cultures with seafood relevant marine species
Dr. Cathy Walsh 
Mote Marine Laboratory
July 10, 2025

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

What does it take to establish stable cell lines from marine species for cultivated seafood applications? In this technical deep dive with Dr. Cathy Walsh of Mote Marine Laboratory, she presents progress in the isolation, culture, and characterization of cells from Pacific white shrimp (Litopenaeus vannamei) and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus).

Dr. Walsh details protocols for obtaining cells from fertilized eggs at the blastomere stage, along with methods for cell isolation and culture. The presentation also includes a review of current efforts to develop continuous cell lines from these species, highlighting specific challenges and technical roadblocks that remain in this area of cellular agriculture research.

This webinar offers valuable insights for researchers working in cultivated seafood and marine cell culture development.

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Meet the speaker:

Dr. Cathy Walsh is a Senior Scientist and Program Manager for the Marine Immunology Program at Mote Marine Laboratory in Sarasota, FL.  She obtained her PhD from Clemson University and has been a research scientist at Mote Marine Laboratory for 34 years. Her research focuses on basic and applied research on the immune systems of marine vertebrates, including cartilaginous fishes (sharks, skate, rays), Florida manatees, and sea turtles. Basic immunological research with marine species explores how immune systems from different species function and potentially lead to novel insights into the evolution of the immune system. Dr. Walsh's current research projects explore how environmental stressors such as red tide toxins, or brevetoxins, can impact immune health of marine species. Other project areas include research on cytotoxic factors produced by cells of the shark immune system that have the potential to benefit human health, and research on the bioactivity of stingray venom. Her more recent research projects focus on the development of cell lines from marine finfish and invertebrates.

Moderator: Amy Huang, Senior Associate Director of Scientific Ecosystems at the Good Food Institute

Titre: From Refugee to U.S. Marine pilot to NASDAQ-listed biotech CEO | Leadership & Fundraising Lessons
Description:
Quang Pham went from being a 10-year-old refugee airlifted out of Vietnam to becoming a Marine pilot, and the CEO of a NASDAQ-listed biotech company. In this conversation, he shares the exact lessons that guided each transition.

Key insights:
On decision-making: “As a young officer, we were taught to make decisions… there’s not enough time to consult with everybody. You gotta make a decision to keep moving and then adjust along the way.” This became his foundational leadership principle across sectors.

On capital discipline: “In the private sector and entrepreneurial world, resources are scarce… you have to treat it with the utmost respect and spend it wisely.” Military spending habits do not translate to startups.

On performance and promotion: “You work hard, but you have to produce results.” Early in his corporate career, he assumed promotions would come automatically. They did not.

On defining success: “You have to follow and pursue what makes you happy. Not what your family or your culture or society wants.” As a Vietnamese refugee, choosing the military was going against all cultural expectations.

On raising capital without pedigree: “I lacked the skills to present to venture capitalists… so I spent a lot of time at Toastmasters picking up new speaking skills.” Within 90 days of leaving his corporate job, he secured venture funding as a first-time CEO.

On pitch strategy: “You have to get to the key points… in the first seven or ten minutes, if not sooner.” Investors have limited attention. He focused his pitch on buyer, payment frequency, and execution, not theoretical market size.

On cold outreach: “It was just three sentences. Who I was, what my company did, something about our common [background].” This approach led to two successful VC rounds.

On leadership transitions: “I knew that I had the skills and the backing and that the baton had to be passed… the company flourished and I was then just a shareholder.” Founders must be willing to step aside to scale.

On AI and decision-making: “There is somebody making decisions for AI, the decision to use AI, the decision to pay for AI… at the end of the day, we still need entrepreneurs and leaders.”

This episode offers practical reflections for those navigating leadership transitions, capital formation, and decision-making in complex, resource-constrained settings.

Titre: Fish Nutrigenomics and Molecular Strategies for Sustainable Aquaculture
Description:
Fish Nutrigenomics and Molecular Strategies for Sustainable Aquaculture

Abstract
The emerging field of fish nutrigenomics bridges nutritional science and molecular biology to explore how dietary inputs influence gene expression, metabolic regulation, and phenotypic outcomes in aquaculture species. This book highlights the molecular underpinnings of fish nutrition, highlighting the application of omics technologies—such as transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics—for evaluating feed efficiency, growth performance, immune response, and environmental resilience in aquatic organisms.

It also examines how environmental stressors interact with feed composition to modulate gene expression, with particular attention to tissue-specific responses in organs like the liver, intestine, gill, and muscle. The book further discusses epigenetic regulation, including DNA methylation and non-coding RNAs, which mediate long-term and potentially transgenerational effects of nutritional programming.

Additionally, it addresses the complexities and opportunities of integrating multi-omics data through systems biology approaches to enable feed optimisation and biomarker discovery.

Special emphasis is placed on the relevance of these insights to tropical aquaculture systems, involving species such as Nile tilapia, African catfish, and Pacific white shrimp. By aligning molecular discoveries with practical feed formulation and selective breeding, this book addresses key knowledge gaps and supports the transition to sustainable, precision-based aquaculture.

It serves not only as an academic reference and technical resource for researchers, educators, and industry stakeholders aiming to apply nutrigenomic approaches to enhance aquaculture productivity, environmental stewardship, and global food security.

\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\

Layman Abstract :
As the global need for seafood rises, fish farming—or aquaculture—is becoming increasingly important. To make it more sustainable and efficient, scientists are exploring a new area called nutrigenomics. This field studies how the food fish eat affects their genes, health, and growth.
This book explains how modern tools like gene and protein analysis help researchers understand how fish respond to different types of feed. By looking inside the fish at the molecular level, scientists can discover which foods help fish grow faster, stay healthier, and better resist stress or disease.
The book highlights key organs like the liver, gut, and muscles, showing how they react to different feeds. It also explores how poor nutrition or bad water can harm fish, and how better diets can improve not just current fish health but possibly future generations through a process called epigenetics.
By combining data on genes, proteins, and metabolism, researchers can create a full picture of how fish bodies work. This helps develop better feeds tailored for commonly farmed species like tilapia, catfish, and shrimp—especially important for food security in tropical regions.
In short, the book shows how using science to understand fish nutrition can help build a healthier, more productive, and eco-friendly aquaculture industry.

Titre: Plongée VR 360 dans l’univers des microalgues marines 🦠
Description:
Encore largement méconnues, les microalgues n’en jouent pas moins un rôle clé dans l’équilibre de la planète en produisant plus de la moitié de l’oxygène que nous respirons. Elles sont aussi le tout premier maillon de la chaîne alimentaire marine. Ces microorganismes renferment par ailleurs des secrets qui pourraient bien révolutionner notre quotidien : ils constituent une source prometteuse de molécules originales pour des applications variées en santé, alimentation humaine et animale, cosmétique, ingénierie de l’environnement…

Le projet CERNUNNOS*, porté par des scientifiques de l’Ifremer, s’inspire d’une méthode développée en agronomie pour améliorer la culture des microalgues sans recourir aux OGM. Grâce à ce film d’animation en réalité virtuelle, plongez dans l’infiniment petit et explorez la méthode de l’hybridation, qui consiste à croiser deux microalgues de la même espèce pour obtenir une descendance cumulant les caractéristiques avantageuses des deux parents. Cette démarche innovante ouvre de nouvelles perspectives pour la société, pour répondre aux enjeux de demain.

Ce film est le fruit d’une collaboration entre l’Ifremer et Atelier Imago Mundi.

Plus d’infos : https://pba.ifremer.fr/Projets/Cernunnos-2020-2024

*Le projet Cernunnos est porté par l’Ifremer et réalisé en collaboration avec la plateforme de cytométrie de l’Université de Nantes (CytoCell). Il est co-financé par la Région des Pays de la Loire (AAP 2020 « Paris Scientifiques ») et l’Ifremer.

Titre: Production de microalgues :  traitement des nitrates, phosphates et CO₂
Description:
Production de microalgues : Une symbiose industrielle gagnant-gagnant pour le traitement des nitrates, phosphates et CO₂

Les méthodes conventionnelles de traitement des eaux usées, telles que la nitrification biologique, la précipitation chimique, l’adsorption ou le traitement par membranes, présentent plusieurs limites : consommation énergétique élevée, production de boues résiduaires difficilement valorisables et coût opérationnel important. En comparaison, la culture de microalgues offre une alternative plus durable et économiquement valorisable.

Par ailleurs, dans un contexte réglementaire de plus en plus strict pour le traitement des eaux, ce procédé alternatif ne dégage pas de gaz à effet de serre (NOx, POx, CO2, CH4).
Les microalgues assimilent directement l’azote et le phosphore présents dans les effluents, réduisant ainsi les rejets tout en captant du CO₂ qui peut également provenir d'activités industrielles. Contrairement aux traitements chimiques nécessitant des réactifs coûteux, ce procédé repose sur un métabolisme naturel, minimisant les intrants et les déchets secondaires. De plus, au lieu de générer des boues nécessitant un traitement supplémentaire, la biomasse algale obtenue peut être valorisée économiquement en fertilisants, biomatériaux, ou alimentation animale, créant ainsi une véritable chaîne de valeur circulaire.

Cette approche, démontré à l’échelle industrielle, permet une réduction efficace des charges polluantes, souvent au-delà des exigences réglementaires. Cette conférence mettra en lumière les avantages opérationnels et environnementaux de ce procédé et explorera les conditions nécessaires à son déploiement à grande échelle.

Titre: Analyse de la compétition entre 2 microalgues : Dunaliella salina et Phaeodactylum tricornutum
Description:
La compétition interspécifique est un des phénomènes écologiques déterminants dans la dynamique des écosystèmes. Au sein des communautés phytoplanctoniques, elle revêt une importance particulière, étant un mécanisme clef pour la diversité et la dynamique du phytoplancton, impactant ses services écologiques comme la séquestration de carbone ou la production d’oxygène. Comprendre ces interactions compétitives est alors essentiel pour surveiller la prolifération de microalgues nuisibles ou bien prédire l’évolution des écosystèmes face aux changements environnementaux. 

Dans cette étude, nous avons cherché à observer ce phénomène de compétition, sous condition contrôlée en laboratoire à l’aide de 2 souches de microalgues : Phaeodactylum tricornutum, une diatomée marine connue pour sa grande plasticité écologique et Dunaliella salina une microalgue verte extrêmement halotolérante. Bien que ces 2 algues ne se rencontrent pas dans le milieu naturel, elles sont régulièrement utilisées en coculture et constituent un modèle idéal pour observer la compétition interspécifique.

Dans un premier temps, nous avons cultivé nos 2 souches dans des milieux à salinité croissante, en condition isolée et en coculture, nous permettant de comparer une croissance sous 2 conditions, la salinité et la compétition. Par la suite, nous avons évalué la répétabilité de notre méthode et la fiabilité de nos résultats à l’aide de tests-statistiques paramétriques et non paramétriques avant de conclure sur l’impact d’un choc salin sur l’interaction compétitive entre D.salina et P.tricornutum. Lors de nos expériences, pour suivre l’évolution de nos populations au fil du temps, nous avons estimé la densité cellulaire de nos milieux à l’aide d’un comptage par cellule de Malassez. Pour des estimations plus fiables, nous utilisons en revanche dans nos résultats des comptages issus de la cytométrie en flux. 

A l’issue de notre étude il apparaît que D.salina soit plus impactée par la compétition que P.tricornutum à raison d’une résistance abiotique favorisée au dépit d’une faible efficacité en compétition directe. A l’aide du test de Kruskal-Wallis, nous avons déterminé que notre méthode d’étude est répétable n’impacte pas l’issue de la compétition entre D.salina et P.tricornutum. Enfin, nous observons avec un stress osmotique que l’halotolérance de D.salina, améliore sa compétitivité dans une situation de compétition indirecte. Au cours de notre étude, nous aurons donc pu observer l’efficacité de P.tricornutum en compétition directe pour l’accès au nutriments et l’efficacité de D.salina en compétition indirecte.

Description: Le projet "Décarboner l’atmosphère par les microalgues" explore l’utilisation des microalgues pour capturer et utiliser le CO₂ (CCU), contribuant à la réduction des gaz à effet de serre. Ce projet allie biologie, chimie verte et engagement écologique, offrant une réflexion sur l'utilisation des microalgues pour lutter contre le changement climatique.

Titre: The fishing industry is in crisis — could lab-grown seafood be the answer?
Description:
As overfishing, ocean pollution and climate change threaten marine ecosystems, lab-grown fish and seafood have been touted by some as a potential solution to the fishing industry's challenges. 

Singapore-based company Umami Bioworks is developing a platform to manufacture cell-based seafood products. 

"We look for species that are endangered, threatened or protected, and have high demand and name recognition from consumers, but that can't be easily grown on farms economically," Mihir Pershad, Umami founder and CEO, told CNBC Tech: The Edge.

The company has focused its efforts on a handful of species, such as eel, bluefin tuna, red snapper, lobster and prawn.  

But unlike other lab-grown food companies, Umami's goal isn't to make a finished product. 

"Our goal is actually selling production capacity, to basically be a technology partner. Our core platform brings together stem cell biology, machine learning and industrial automation," Pershad said. 

Umami hopes to begin commercialization in 2025. 

In 2023, it teamed up with Israeli company Steakholder Foods to produce the world's first 3D printed lab-grown fish fillet, and it is currently working with a Malaysian biotechnology company to bring the first large-scale cultivated food factory to Southeast Asia.

Partnerships like these will be key to ensure the sustainability of Asia's aquaculture industry, which accounts for 92% of global production.

Description:
We know meat is problematic for the environment, and seafood has its own issues with overfishing, so do we have to wave goodbye to the foods we love?



Well, what if we told you that there are substitutes which you can enjoy without sacrificing taste and texture?



We start with mycoprotein, in the form of the well-known meat substitute products of Quorn Foods (https://www.quorn.co.uk/?msclkid=ce16ff0dcf8911eca9c95c07d51cdd9d) . Tim Finnigan, Chief Scientific Advisor for Quorn Foods, explains why mycoprotein is such a suitable source of protein, how it is manufactured, the environmental benefits, and how fusarium venenatum, the microfungus, was discovered. And... it's tasty!



In the same episode, we ask Dr Lauran Madden, Chief Technology Officer at BlueNalu (https://www.bluenalu.com/) , to share with you the engineering process, the health and environmental benefits, and the positive impact on the environment of their cell-cultured seafood. This is hugely critical as the populations of marine species have halved since 1970, battling with overfishing, illegal fishing, and the effects of trawling. This cell-cultured seafood comes first...plaice... *sorry*.



By the end of this episode, we will hopefully have demonstrated the environmental and health benefits of switching meat out of our diets for better alternatives.

Se refiere a organismos modificados genéticamente en laboratorio.
Al principio causó temor por sus posibles incidencias con respecto a la saludos de los seres humanos y de las otras especies vivientes.
Se la clasifica por colores para distinguir su ámbito de acción.
Biotecnología Roja: Se relaciona con la medicina, producción de vacunas y fármacos. Biotecnología Blanca: Se aplica en la industria para obtener plásticos biodegradables.
Biotecnología Verde: se aplica en los cultivos vegetales para lograr mayores rendimientos.
Biotecnología Azul: Se aplica en ambientes acuáticos y marinos, todavía poco desarrollada.
Tiene una gran importancia geográfica en muchos aspectos.
Hay muchos ejemplos de genes que se trasladan entre vegetales; y entre vegetales y animales.

“Our seafood supply is also increasingly contaminated with heavy metals, microplastics, parasites, and antibiotics and global fishing contributes more GHG emissions than the entire aviation sector. We need novel, more sustainable methods to produce the additional 100 million tons of seafood needed by 2050 if we are to feed humanity while preserving and restoring our planet. 



"At Umami Meats, we are developing a platform for producing cultivated, 'not caught' seafood to enable local, price competitive production of cultivated fish that keeps endangered species in the ocean while providing consumers with delicious, healthy, low emissions, sustainable seafood. 



“We are dedicated to regenerating our oceans and our planet by enabling consumers to have their fish and eat it too, starting with IUCN Red Listed species that are difficult to farm and that are being driven extinct by human consumption. 



“Our goal is to be the "Intel inside" the seafood industry to allow traditional seafood suppliers to produce millions of tons of cultivated seafood that help them overcome dwindling traditional supply, meet growing demand, and establish a food system that is sustainable for the next century and beyond." 



Mihir has an academic background in protein biochemistry and has spent his career working to commercialize deep tech innovations to address humanity's grand challenges. Most recently, he was a Venture Partner at Early Charm Ventures, where he led the commercialization of university spinouts at the intersection of biotechnology and aquaculture. Mihir is also author of Cultivated Abundance, a book that outlines a framework for entrepreneurs to leverage transformative technologies to build an inspiring, abundant future for humanity.

Titre: Pisciculture durable en Amazonie
Description:
Renforcer la capacité des petits pisciculteurs de l’Amazonie péruvienne à maitriser leur outil de production à travers l’élevage durable et l’utilisation d’insectes dans l’alimentation de poissons.Les pisciculteurs formés parviennent à augmenter leur productivité, à réduire et le recours à d’autres sources d’aliments protéinés et à vendre une partie de leur production.Le projet repose sur le transfert d’une technique innovante développée par l’IRD (Michel Sauvain) et ses partenaires à l’Université Péruvienne Cayetano Heredia – UPCH (Denis Castillo, Estrellita Díaz et al.) avec la collaboration sur ce projet de l’Institut de Recherche de l’Amazonie Péruvienne - IIAP (Miriam Alván, , Harvey Satayala et al.) 
Cette technique consiste à élever des larves d’insectes produites par le recyclage des déchets organiques de l’agriculture locale et à les utiliser comme aliments des poissons en aquaculture à travers l’élevage de la gamitana, poisson particulièrement consommé en Amazonie. Elle contribuera non seulement à réduire les coûts de production, mais elle favorisera aussi la préservation de la biodiversité, en limitant le recours à l’exploitation intensive de poissons et insectes prélevés dans les milieux naturels contribuant à leur dégradation.

Reforzar la capacidad de los pequeños piscicultores de la Amazonia peruana para controlar su producción mediante la cría sostenible y la utilización de insectos en la alimentación de los peces. Los piscicultores formados pueden aumentar su productividad, reducir la necesidad de otras fuentes de alimentación proteínica y vender parte de su producción. El proyecto se basa en la transferencia de una técnica innovadora desarrollada por el IRD (Michel Sauvain) y sus socios de la Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia - UPCH (Denis Castillo, Estrellita Díaz et al. ) con la colaboración en este proyecto del Instituto de Investigaciones de la Amazonía Peruana - IIAP (Miriam Alván, Harvey Satayala et al.). Esto no sólo ayudará a reducir los costos de producción, sino también a preservar la biodiversidad, al limitar la necesidad de una explotación intensiva de peces e insectos extraídos de entornos naturales, contribuyendo así a su degradación. Titre: Discovery Matters | Ep54. Mycoprotein v. cell-cultured seafood
Description:
We know meat is problematic for the environment, and seafood has its own issues with overfishing, so do we have to wave goodbye to the foods we love?

Well, what if we told you that there are substitutes which you can enjoy without sacrificing taste and texture?

We start with mycoprotein, in the form of the well-known meat substitute products of Quorn Foods. Tim Finnigan, Chief Scientific Advisor for Quorn Foods, explains why mycoprotein is such a suitable source of protein, how it is manufactured, the environmental benefits, and how fusarium venenatum, the microfungus, was discovered. And... it's tasty!

In the same episode, we ask Dr Lauran Madden, Chief Technology Officer at BlueNalu, to share with you the engineering process, the health and environmental benefits, and the positive impact on the environment of their cell-cultured seafood. This is hugely critical as the populations of marine species have halved since 1970, battling with overfishing, illegal fishing, and the effects of trawling. This cell-cultured seafood comes first...plaice... *sorry*.

By the end of this episode, we will hopefully have demonstrated the environmental and health benefits of switching meat out of our diets for better alternatives.

Recorded in 2022.

Titre: Caroline Roose dans le débat "Vers un secteur des algues de l’Union fort et durable"
Description:
Jeudi 11 mai, Caroline Roose est intervenue dans le débat "Vers un secteur des algues de l’Union fort et durable".

Son intervention ⬇️

"Avec cette résolution, le Parlement envoie un signal fort en faveur de la culture des algues en Europe. Son développement présente de nombreux intérêts. 
Les algues sont une alternative aux farines de poisson utilisées en aquaculture et qui entraînent le pillage 
des mers en Afrique de l'Ouest. Mais les algues sont aussi intéressantes pour la consommation humaine. Un aliment nutritif et durable. La culture de macro-algues séquestre du carbone et contribue à la lutte contre le changement climatique. Elle peut aussi contribuer à la restauration des écosystèmes marins. La culture d'algues peut permettre à certains pêcheurs de se diversifier au niveau de leur activité, mais il faudra veiller à ce que la culture d'algues reste durable.
Éviter la collecte d'algues via des techniques destructrices comme les dragues et privilégier des méthodes moins impactantes. Cultiver des espèces locales. Éviter des monocultures d'algues, qui présenteraient des risques sanitaires. Donc, développons donc 
la culture d'algues, mais évitons de répéter les dérives de l'aquaculture intensive."

Description:
AUTEUR : Pierre Feillet est Directeur de recherche émérite à l'INRAE, membre de l'Académie d'agriculture, membre de l'Académie des technologies

VERSION ECRITE : Rejoindre le site web de l'académie des Sciences et Lettres de Montpellier, cliquez sur "chercher un document",  introduire le code conférence :  4671.

RESUME : Les industries manufacturières vont-elles remplacer la terre nourricière ? Les ingénieurs et les chimistes vont-ils se substituer aux agriculteurs ? Cauchemar ou rêve d’un monde d’où la faim aura disparu ? 
De nombreux facteurs poussent à l’apparition de nouvelles manières de produire des aliments et de se nourrir : l’évolution de la démographie (croissance, vieillissement, urbanisation et niveau de vie des populations), la diminution du nombre de paysans, l’impact d’une agriculture productiviste sur l’environnement, le changement climatique, la disponibilité de sols fertiles, un nouveau regard sur le bien-être des animaux, la recherche d’une alimentation plus « végétalisée », les avancées des sciences et des technologies. 
Fort de cette analyse, des scientifiques, des entrepreneurs et des investisseurs sont nombreux à croire à l’avenir des hachis végétaux substituts de la viande, des farines protéinées de larves d’insectes, des viandes fabriquées par cultures de cellules souches, des laits artificiels issus de microorganismes génétiquement modifiés. Des milliards de dollars sont investis dans des start-up dont les « nouveaux aliments » commencent à être commercialisés sur tous les continents.

The food technology company Bluu Seafood (formerly Bluu Biosciences) is the first company in Europe to specialize in the commercial production of cultivated fish. Titre: Discovery Matters | Ep54. Mycoprotein v. cell-cultured seafood
Description:
We know meat is problematic for the environment, and seafood has its own issues with overfishing, so do we have to wave goodbye to the foods we love?

Well, what if we told you that there are substitutes which you can enjoy without sacrificing taste and texture?

We start with mycoprotein, in the form of the well-known meat substitute products of Quorn Foods. Tim Finnigan, Chief Scientific Advisor for Quorn Foods, explains why mycoprotein is such a suitable source of protein, how it is manufactured, the environmental benefits, and how fusarium venenatum, the microfungus, was discovered. And... it's tasty!

In the same episode, we ask Dr Lauran Madden, Chief Technology Officer at BlueNalu, to share with you the engineering process, the health and environmental benefits, and the positive impact on the environment of their cell-cultured seafood. This is hugely critical as the populations of marine species have halved since 1970, battling with overfishing, illegal fishing, and the effects of trawling. This cell-cultured seafood comes first...plaice... *sorry*.

By the end of this episode, we will hopefully have demonstrated the environmental and health benefits of switching meat out of our diets for better alternatives.

Titre: A Whale of a Tale: Wildtype and the Future of Cultivated Seafood
Description:
As we continue to empty the oceans, our species’ demand for fish only seems to increase. But what if we could eat all the bluefin tuna and salmon we wanted without having to harm fish and other aquatic animals?

 That’s the vision that companies like Wildtype are working toward. Founded in 2016, this cultivated fish startup has raised $120 million so far and now has 60 employees who are growing real fish meat without the fish. I’ve enjoyed their product now twice, both pre-pandemic and recently, and enjoyed it both times. 

 Wild Type salmon that I recently enjoyed while in their San Francisco HQ.

 Today, Wildtype is building serious cultivation capacity to help turn the tide for the oceans, and in this episode, we discuss the company’s origins, the role bird poop played, and what the company’s up to today. We even discuss the co-founders’ first company idea which they abandoned in favor of Wildtype: a redesigned Neti pot that would’ve been called The Schnozel. (They never trademarked this, so maybe one day you’ll be able to buy that Schnozel of your dreams.)

 In addition to chatting about whether it’s faster and cheaper to grow fish cells compared to mammalian and avian cells, co-founders Justin and Arye open up about what impact it’s had on their personal lives to have gone from normal jobs to running their own company. We also talk about the perennial question in this industry: If the FDA gave them approval today, how soon would it be before we see Wildtype fish on restaurant menus?

 Discussed in this episode

  Our  past episode with BlueNalu New Harvest founder Jason Matheny recently became CEO of the Rand Corporation The 2018 book  Clean Meat (still highly relevant!) Bored Cow’s great chocolate milk made with Perfect Day’s animal-free whey protein  More about Justin Kolbeck and Aryé Elfenbein

 Justin Kolbeck is co-founder and CEO of Wildtype, which is on a mission to create the cleanest, most sustainable seafood on the planet. Before Wildtype, he spent nearly five years as a consultant at Strategy& (not a typo!) helping companies develop and launch products, grow into new markets, and operate efficiently. Justin started his career as a Foreign Service Officer, serving in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Australia, and Washington DC.  He is a graduate of the Yale School of Management, L’Institut d’Études Politiques de Paris, and UC Berkeley.

 Aryé Elfenbein is co-founder of Wildtype, where he directs the company’s scientific research. Aryé completed his MD and PhD at Dartmouth and Kyoto University; he completed his clinical training in internal medicine and cardiology at Yale. Prior to Wildtype, he completed a fellowship in regenerative cardiovascular medicine research at the Gladstone Institutes / UCSF. He currently practices cardiology in the critical care setting.

Titre: Can We Grow Salmon Without The Fish? | Dr. Arye Elfenbein, MD, PhD
Description:
Imagine enjoying salmon produced from fish cells rather than harvesting a fish from the ocean. Dr. Arye Elfenbein explores the science behind cultivated seafood and the challenges of building a new food production system.

Dr. Arye Elfenbein, MD, PhD, is the Co-Founder of Wildtype ( https://www.wildtypefoods.com/ ), a biotechnology company which produces cultured seafood (with a focus on cultivated Pacific salmon) from fish cells, sustainably and cost effectively, with the nutritional benefits, but without common contaminants such as mercury, microplastics, antibiotics, or pesticides, and without relying on commercial fishing or fish farming.

Born in Israel and raised in Australia, Dr. Elfenbein combines his deep passion for medicine and unique childhood connection to the ocean to fuel Wildtype’s health and environmental mission. 

After studying at Dartmouth and Kyoto University, attaining a PhD and MD, Dr. Elfenbein began his residency at Yale where he first trained in Internal Medicine before completing training in Cardiology. After residency, he moved to San Francisco to work with Professor Dr. Deepak Srivastava at the revered Gladstone Institutes / UCSF, also known for being the scientific homes of Nobel laureates Dr. Shinya Yamanaka (iPs cells) and Dr. Jennifer Doudna (CRISPR).
  
During his time at the Gladstone Institutes, Dr. Elfenbein’s research focused on cardiac regeneration following heart attacks. This research inspired him to apply the principles of stem cell biology beyond medicine, and to address the growing problems in our food system. 

When away from Wildtype, Dr. Elfenbein continues to work as a cardiologist with a focus on critical care, lending his expertise and passion for patient care to the ICU.

Titre: Webinar: A Conversation on Cell-Cultured Meat
Description:
It goes by many names: cultured, cell-based, cultivated, or lab-grown meat. All are meat alternatives made in lab vats via animal cells and a cultured medium, like fetal bovine serum or a secret proprietary mix. There are currently more than 70 companies planning to bring cell-cultured “meat” to market that mimics the form of chicken, beef, pork, seafood, and even pet food! These companies are promoting this new technique as a way to cultivate a meat alternative that is supposedly “cleaner” and safer than traditional meat. 

The webinar will cover questions like: 

— How will cell-cultured "meat" be cultivated at a large scale? 
— Is cell-cultured meat really made through an environmentally friendly production model? 
— How will these novel products be properly regulated? 
— How will claims of “intellectual property” hinder production transparency? 
— Who is investing in lab-grown meat and what are their motives? 

Speakers:

Dr. Michael Hansen, Senior Staff Scientist, Consumer's Union 

As Consumer Reports’ Senior Staff Scientist, Mike Hansen, Ph.D., has been sharing his scientific expertise for more than 20 years. He develops policy positions, testifies before government agencies, speaks widely at conferences in the U.S. and abroad, and talks frequently to media on critical food safety and environmental health concerns, including mad cow disease, genetic engineering, pesticide use, and antibiotics in animal feed. A biologist and ecologist who did his Ph.D. in the techniques of Integrated Pest Management, he has a unique perspective on genetically engineered mosquitoes. 

Tom Neltner, Chemical Policy Director, Environmental Defense Fund 

As EDF’s Chemicals Policy Director, Tom Neltner leads efforts to remove or minimize hazardous chemicals from products and the marketplace through cross-cutting policy initiatives. His primary focus is on food additive safety, where he promotes corporate partnerships and advances federal regulatory efforts to improve public health and the environment, and on lead where he works to advance legislative, regulatory and collaborative efforts to reduce lead exposure. He supports EDF’s work on chemical safety, especially lead, formaldehyde, and hazardous materials management. 

Julia Ranney, Research and Policy Associate, Center for Food Safety 

As CFS’s Research and Policy Associate, Julia has been researching who has been funding the lab-grown meat industry and what their motives might be. While getting her B.A. in Politics from Oberlin College, she studied food security and sustainability abroad in four different countries and eventually wrote her thesis about the Green Revolution in Africa. 

The webinar is moderated by CFS’s Regional Development Director Ashley Lukens, Ph.D.

Originally held via Zoom on June 21, 2022. TAKE ACTION: Tell FDA to Institute Strong Regulations of Cell-Cultured "Meat": https://action.centerforfoodsafety.org/a/tell-fda-to-institute-strong-regulations-of-cell-cultured-meat

Titre: Bluefin Foods creates a better solution to supply the world with cell-cultured seafood and meat
Description:
Bluefin Foods Inc., which is part of the Magnify incubator at the California NanoSystems Institute at UCLA (CNSI) is a cell-cultured seafood company focused on bringing bluefin tuna sushi products to all the sushi lovers in the world. 

The startup company was the winner of the Easton Technology Management Center “Cross-Campus Innovation Challenge” at the Anderson School of Management last spring. The competition invites students to solve real-world problems and Bluefin Foods, co-founded by two Anderson MBA students, answered the call. The 2022 competition is now open for applications at: https://www.anderson.ucla.edu/about/centers/easton-technology-management-center/for-students/innovation-challenge

“Ultimately, we are creating a better solution to supply the world with meat food products,” said Bluefin Foods co-founder Keith David. Adds Bluefin Foods other co-founder, Taissa Maleh,  “We are developing a high-quality and cost-effective process of producing cell-cultured seafood to be a viable alternative to the traditional seafood supply chain.”

Bluefin Foods success is a prime example of the benefits of cross-campus  and student research collaboration at UCLA.  Additionally, the company makes use of key resources needed to establish a successful commercial enterprise that are available to start-up companies through incubators such as CNSI’s Magnify.

Titre: Dr. Reza Ovissipour: Optimizing media development for cultivated seafood
Description:
Seminar Series: The Science of Alt. Protein
Optimizing media development for cultivated seafood
November 10th, 2021

Join us to learn from Dr. Reza Ovissipour about his GFI-funded work to develop and optimize novel media for the production of cultivated seafood. Through the use of Response Surface Methodology (RSM), as well as artificial neural networks, Reza's lab is fine-tuning cell culture media to enable fish cells to not only grow but thrive.

Dr. Ovissipour also discusses his role in the newly formed National Institute for Cellular Agriculture, a USDA-funded project that aims to develop new adoptable techno-economically viable cultivated meat systems and develop new educational platforms for training future professionals.

Meet the speaker:
Dr. Ovissipour is an Assistant Professor in Cellular Agriculture in the Department of Food Science and Technology (FST), and the Virginia Seafood AREC at Virginia Tech. He also holds a faculty appointment with Genetics, Bioinformatics, and Computational Biology; Center for Advanced Innovation in Agriculture; and Center for Emerging, Zoonotic, and Arthropod-borne Pathogens. Reza’s program, the FutureFoods Lab and Cellular Agriculture Initiative, focuses on alternative proteins, cell line development, media optimization, and scaffold development.

Moderator: Amy Huang, University Innovation Manager, The Good Food Institute

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

About The Good Food Institute:
The Good Food Institute (GFI) is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit working internationally to make alternative proteins like plant-based and cultivated meat delicious, affordable, and accessible. GFI advances open-access research, mobilizes resources and talent, and empowers partners across the food system to create a sustainable, secure, and just protein supply.

Learn more at https://gfi.org/​ 

Want to join our good food community? Visit https://gfi.org/community/​
GFIdeas is a community for entrepreneurs, scientists, students, and subject matter experts who are driving alternative protein innovation. Each month, we host two online seminars with leading science and business experts from around the world. In addition to our seminars, networking events, and community Slack, we also have a monthly newsletter that shares timely opportunities and developments in the good food world.

Hence, the need for sustainable and healthy food and protein sources is crucial. Seafood is a widely consumed protein in this part of the world. The innovation in the alternative protein sector for red and white meat is immense but the alternative seafood sector is vast and only recently disruption has started for plant-based and cell-based seafood. That is exactly what we are addressing at Shiok Meats, the first cell-based meat company in Singapore and South East Asia. At Shiok Meats, the world’s first cell-based crustacean meat company, our mission is to bring delicious, clean and healthy seafood and meats by harvesting from cells instead of animals. Shiok Meats will bring cell-based crustacean meats (shrimp, crab, lobster) to your table in the next couple of years. Titre: Conférence : Les algues et leurs bienfaits pour la santé et la nutrition | U'Cook 2021
Description:
La 5ème édition d’U’Cook-Innovation 100% digitale, organisée par l’UCO Bretagne Nord, a eu lieu le 19 mars 2021 sur le thème des « ALGUES : une solution d’avenir ».


CONFERENCE 2021 : « Les algues et leurs bienfaits pour la santé et la nutrition »
Animée par Anne-Sophie BURLOT / Chargée de projets en R&D Sourcing, Olmix


PARCOURS PROFESSIONNEL :
Ayant toujours été attirée par la valorisation des végétaux pour la santé et la nutrition, j’ai suivi un parcours universitaire classique, de la licence au doctorat. Tout au long de ces 8 années d’étude, je me suis spécialisée dans les biotechnologies et me suis rapprochée de la mer que je n’ai jamais vraiment quittée, étant Bretonne d’origine.

Depuis 2013, je travaille sur les algues vertes et rouges qui se trouvent en abondance sur les côtes Bretonnes. J’ai saisi les opportunités qui m’étaient offertes pour me rendre dans des centres de recherche au Canada, au Mexique et au Sénégal où j’ai acquis des connaissances et des compétences sur la culture d’algues et leur valorisation pour divers champs d’applications. Connaissant le potentiel des algues, j’ai voulu me positionner en tant qu’intermédiaire entre leur exploitation raisonnée et leur préservation et conservation écologique. Ainsi, j’ai intégré le groupe Olmix en 2018 en tant que chargée de projet en R&D. Mon travail contribue à assurer l’approvisionnement en matière première algale à l’entreprise selon une gestion durable de la ressource.


RÉSUME DE L’INTERVENTION :
Plus de 220 espèces d’algues sont exploitées à l’heure actuelle dans le monde et près de 70 % de ces espèces sont valorisées pour la nutrition et pour leurs bienfaits sur la santé. La plupart des algues sont caractérisées par des teneurs importantes en fibres alimentaires et en minéraux et par une petite quantité de matière grasse. De plus, leur composition protéique ainsi que les activités antioxydantes mesurées et liées à la présence de composés phénoliques font des algues une ressource attrayante pour de nombreuses applications en particulier pour l’alimentation humaine, animale et végétale.
